THE SIEGE AND SUB RENDER OF BOM A US UN D The tower of Bomarsund, which, judging from the ruins, must have been one ot considerable extent, was completely burnt to the ground by the Russian garrison, about three weeks ago, from an apprehension that it might afford shelter to the besiegers. Aftef its destruction there was nothing left but the forts, and they stood in something like the following order. Close upon the shore was a low range of fortifications about forty feet in height, mounting eighty guns in two tiers. On a hill above, about a mile and a half inland, was a round tower, also furnished with two tiers of guns ; to the west of this, upon a hill of still greater elevation, was another round tower, similar in every respect to the other ; and on the extreme east, also upon a hill, stood a third tower, like the two former. Each of these buildings mounted from twenty to thirty guns of considerable size and power. There were, four forts in all, each of which presented to the non-professional eye a ra- in ther formidable appearance. The hay front took the form of a semicircle, the diameter of which might be about three miles. From the centre of the bay the batteries stood about north, and the ships of war, steamers, and transports, stretched across from the east to the western shore. The ships so moored were : þÿ English ; Bulldog (flag Sir O Napier), Edinburgh (flag Admiral Chads), Hogue, Ajax, Blenheim, Amphion, Termagant, Bclleisle (hospital ship). Penelope, Sphynx, Gla-

diator, Valorous, Vulture, Pigmy, Lightning. The troops transports were the Prince, Julia. Columbia. Cornelius Fox, besides several yachts and cutters. French: Inflexible (flag). Breslau. Trident, Tagc, Duperre, St. Louis, Algerine (hospital ship). Phlegclhon, Darien. Souffleur, Asmodec, and the imperial yacht. The Leopard, A rrogant, Odin, Hecla, Locust, Porcupine, Otter. Alban, and Cuckoo were stationed on the north side of the island. # On Sunday the 13th, the French began the bombardment of the western tower in reality. The fort, however, was the first to open fire, which it did at four in the morning, as the Chasseurs, with their field pieces, were crossing the valley. Four mortars were fired at the base of a gentle slope, and four long brass guns, sixteen-pounders, in the batteries, at point blank upon the fort. They soon obtained a capital range, nnd a great cannonade was maintained for many hours. Numerous shells burst in the embrasures and upon the roof, and by ten o'clock considerable portions of the lower were battered down ; but still no practicable breach had been made. The Russians threw shell into the French lines with some effect. About four þÿo clock a flag of truce was hung out of an embrasure. General Paraguay þÿd Hilliers thereupon proceeded up to within ten yards of the fort, with a company of Chasseurs as bis guard. The

enemy demanded two þÿhours respite to bury their dead. The general gave them one hour only, and the use they made of this was, to gain reinforcements from the fort below, and to obtain a further supply of ammunition. It is said the enemy fired upon the guard. It is needless to state the result of this treachery. The firing recommenced with redoubled fury, the shells being most effective in their descent, and the riflemen on the rocks pouring into the embrasures a deadly shower of bullets. The eastern tower now sent shells completely over the besieged fort into the camp of the allies. At eight p. m. another flag of truce was offered, but the general replied, þÿ Certainly not ; these men have not respected the object of (heir truce, and they shall not receive the slightest consideration. Continue the bomþÿbardment. A terrific shower of shot, shell, and musketry therefore continued all night from both sides, but at half-past five the tower fell into the hands of its brave assailants. The French immediately planted the tricolour upon it. When they entered the fort, it is said, they found the whole garrison, officers as well as men. raving drunk. Considering the provocation they had received, our allies acted with admirable moderation, for only one Russian was bayoneted, and this because he had struck an officer after surrendering. The loss of the Russians was found to be very considerable. On the morning of Tuesday, the 15th, the eastern tower was attacked by the English shore battery, which was manned by seamen

and marines from the Edinburgh, the llogue, the Ajax and the Blenheim, under the command of Captain Ramsay. Some of the ships were also engaged, and this being the day of th e/ele de Napoletm, a royal salute was fired, the honours being paid with shotted guns. The long fort was engaged, and it suffered severely front our guns. By half-past four in the afternoon the guns of the eastern tower were silenced ; at six a flag of truce appeared, and the marines and blue jackets took possession. During the attack Lieutenant Wrotieslev, R. E , was killed. He was stooping down in obedience to signal when a cannon ball, after striking the trunnion of one of the guns, bounded against him, inflicting a dreadful wound. His side was crushed, and his hands, which were folded together at the time, were torn to pieces; he died very soon afterwards, on board the Belleislo. In this fort there were six killed and seven wounded, and 125 were made prisoners. Captain Ramsay was slightly wounded. The prisoners weie sent on board the Termagant. Today the western tower blew up, whether from accident or design is not known. On the lGlh (Wednesday) the long fort was attacked by the Edinburgh, the Ajax, and the steamers, at long range. Meanwhile the shore batteries were advanced considerably nearer to the land-face of the fort, and kept up an incessant fire ; the heavy guns in the six-gun battery, served by the English tinder Captain Pelham, did great execution ; large blocks ol granite, forming the face of

the fort, which, in appearance, offered an immense resistance, fell out in masses, and the rubble with .which the wall was filled in tumbled out in heaps. At the same time t he Leopard attacked the fort of Presto, on the other side the narrow channel At 12-30 a flag of truce was held out at an embrasure towards the fleet A boat, with Captain Hall, of the Bulldog, was sent on shore, and at half-past twelve the governor surrendered, and the troops laid down their arms Two thousand prisoners were taken, who will be conveyed to England. General Bodisco, the governor, is an old man, apparently 80 years of age. He was very anxious that the French gencral-inchief should certify that he had done his duly. General Baraguay þÿd Hilliersreturned his sword, and at the same time extolled the valour with which he had defended his trust, and the prudence which had surrendered it when further resistance could have done no more than cause a useless waste of life. The Russian general then sent a priest to the officer in command of Presto Fort, with orders

8 Alt to surrender. The order was obeyed ; and thus the four forts of Bomarsund fell into the possession of the allies. l Many Russians were suffocated in the Bo- j marsund casemates by the smoke of their own fire. After the surrender there were great rejoicings in Aland, and prayers were offered in the churches for Queen Victoria and the Emperor Louis Napoleon The fortress was found to contain ammunition and provisions for one year.

POLITICAL DEMONSTRATION AT COPENHAGEN. A crowded meeting of the members of the Constitutional Society was held in Copenhagen, on Tuesday evening. Three thousand persons, including men of all ranks, were present. Enthusiastic resolutions were passed, supporting the ground-law, denouncing the despotism of the octroi, and defying the Ministry. All the persons present solemnly agreed to sustain the Parliament in impeaching the Cabinet, and to refuse the payment of taxes until this step had been taken. A sum, amounting to several thousand dollars, was subscribed in the room towards forming a fund for guaranteeing the support of discharged civilians, members of Parliament, and for assisting the Constitutional press. The name of the King was not mentioned during the proceedings. At the close, loud cheers were given for the Constitution. The ; Ministry continue to threaten obnoxious public men, as well as members of Parliament holding office. Theconsequcnee is, that fresh resignations are taking 1 place. þÿ London Illustrated News, Sep. 2.

A draft of an ordinance extending the Law of the 11th March 1851 to the Danish Westiudiu Islands has been laid before the Colonial Council by the Government for the deliberation of the Council. Totally concurring with the reasons on which the draft is founded, the Council have unanimously witli Id votes agreed upon recommending it with the hereafter mentioned amend ments and additions ad 2. in order that the reorganisation of the post establishment in the Colonies proposed in the draft may cover its expenses, it will probably he necessary, that all matters appertaining thereto he arranged in such a manner, that it will he not only convenient but also cheap for the public to make use of the post. With regard to this point it might have to he taken into consideration, that people here are generally accustomed to get their letters conveyed from one island to the other without any expense whatever, and moreover accustomed to regard the unsafety of this convey ance partly counterbalanced by the fact that it i attended without expense. The Colonial Council are of opinion, that the postage contained in paragraph 2 and paragraph 0 (for a single letter -1 Cents or by post-stamp 3 Cents and 1 Cent for the delivery) will collectively he too high, and that moreover the fee for delivery does not correspond with the principle

hid down in the law of 1 1th March 1851. Also it would, no doubt, he requisite for promoting the use of post-stamps, that some reduction in the price he allowed on the purchase of a larger number of them at a time. If the fee stipulated in paragraph 6 for the delivery of letters be taken off, the postage of 4 Cents for a single letter without post-stamp according to paragraph 2 will answer, provided that a reduction of 5 Cents be allowed when 10 poststamps are bought at a time. To confine this allowance to the purchase of a greater number I than 10 stamps at a time, would probably deprive it of practical effect. Report to Bli Hajcsly On the draft of an ordinance concerning an Extra Tax to cover the Expenses of the Land-treasury of St. Thomas, caused by the Cholera Epidemic With reference to the preambles to the above mentioned draft the Colonial Council beg leave to observe, that when the Cholera Epidemic broke out at St. Thomas no preparations whatever had been provided to guard against or alleviate the calamity, and moreover the Land-treasury was destitute of means for defraying those expenditures generally imposed on it, whereforo tho Communal Administration, from the urgent necessity of having immediate recourse to sanitary measures, was necessitated to make use of a fund of $20,513 89, which had been deposited in the Land Chest, which sum in conformity with a Government þÿGeneral s placard of 20th February 1845 had been collected by assessment on the Commune for tho special purpose of defraying the expenses in erecting a communal hospital as well as a gaol. The intention of the proposed extra-tax is to procure the amount of this fund. During the detailed discussnns of this subject in the Colonial Council the following amendments have by a majority been agreed upon, viz : ad 1 . With 8 votes against 7, that after the words þÿ þÿextra-tax be inserted : þÿ an amount of 2000 West India þÿDollars, and with the same number of votes, that there be added : þÿ the extra-tax to be paid in two succeeding years, one half þÿannually, and ad 2. With 9 votes against 6, that instead of tho figure þÿ þÿ15 be put þÿ þÿ18.

Meanwhile as regards the draft in toto, the Council have, with a majority of 9 votes against 6, agreed upon disreconimending its being made law, in which respect the following remarks have been made :

The Cholera Epidemic has materially impaired the income of many of the inhabitants of St. Thomas ; the opulent merchants and the middle order of people as well as the common mechanics have suffered considerably from the stagnation of business for several months during the prevalence of the Epidemic and long after it had ceased. An extra-tax eannot be expected to be received with good will by the majority of the inhabitants of the island. It cannot be considered indispensably necessary to collect so large an amount as is proposed here, because a communal hospital, however greatly desirable, is by no means absolutely necessary. In the Colonies as well as elsewhere it certainly ought to be a standing principle, not to impose new taxes on the inhabitants when not indispensably necessary, which in the present case would be difficult to be proved, and that at a time when a tax þÿ in favor of (he Land-treasury of St. Thoþÿmas has already been adopted by the Colonial Council, which tax will yield an annual increase of the revenues above $7000. According to the preambles to the last mentioned tax to the Land-treasury the Burgher Council have stated as their opinion : ad 1 that the tax mentioned herein will in- crease the Store-tax with - - - - þÿ $ 3,600 ad 2 that the alterations proposed with regard to the lamp tax þÿ4 -> will give an increase of----------- 1 >300 ad 3 and 4 the tax on horses and carriages 1,500 ad boats may be calculated at - - 5 the tax on smaller vessels and - - - 920

Deducting from this sum the amount of the þÿCountry-treasury annual s deficiency 1,320 there will appear an annual surplus - $6,000 - If the building of an hospital be delayed for a few years, a sufficient amount may be had annually out of the said surplus $6000 for refunding the hospital fund without even deferring other requisite improvements. Experience has unfortunately proved, that it is not proper that large capitals be deposited in the Country-treasury. Already in the years 1829 to 1831 inclusive a double-tax was assessed in St. Thomas for the purpose of procuring funds for building a Custom-house ; the sum collected (10,500 Pa.) was made over to the fund for repairing streets 4-c., and the Custom-house has not yet been built. In the year 1845 the inhabitants of St. Thomas were again assessed with a double tax and imposts for the purpose of building an hospital, by which means the amount in question $20,513 89 was collected, this sum has likewise been applied contrary to its intention. It was first encroached upon at different times, to the amount of $4,900 for covering the þÿLand-treasury deficiency, s and the balance has now been used during the Cholera Epidemic- Thus, experience does not even offer any guarantee, that the hospital will actually be built, if even the means be raised immediately, and this ought the more to be taken into consideration, as it is not yet finally decided at what place or according to what plan the hospital is to be built. But even losing sight of, that at present it is

not indispensably necessary that an hospital be erected, the Colonial Council would hesitate to assess an extra tax according to the plan proposed in the draft. The assessment of the amount on each individual would necessarily give rise to arbitrariness ; and to extend the taxation to the lower olasses would be not only quite uncommon, but even in so far unjust, because just these classes of the community have suffered most by the Cholera Epidemic. Nor can the Colonial Council admit, that a

In consequence of the draft of an ordinance relative to the assessment of several taxes in the island of St. Croix to the Land-treasury, which has been produced by the Government, the Colonial Council beg leave most submissively to observe : that notwithstanding existing circumstances in the island may render it a matter of hesitation to impose more taxes or duties than those already levied, and which in many cases are collected with difficulty, yet it must be acknowledged, that as long as no effectual retrenchments of the expenditure of the Land-treasury can be effected, it is necessary to provide means for covering the difference between the revenues and disbursements. We consider the proposed taxes in general þÿ reserving some additions and alterations hereafter mentioned þÿ proper and equitable, especially as thereby a number of individuals in the community, who heretofore have not contributed to defray the necessary expenses of the public, will be assessed with a part thereof. With special regard to, that the proposed imposts will not be sufficient to cover the amount required, we beg leave to observe

ad 1. That the additional duty of 3 per Cent ought likewise to be levied on the import-duties. According to elucidations received, the amount of these duties may be put at about $50,000 annually, and the said additional duty will thus yield .ii inconsiderable contribution to the amount to bo raised, aud the payment thereof be equitably apportioned among all the inhabitants of the island, according to the greater or less consumption of the articles imported, aud could not be felt oppressive or burthen onto, as per instance : the import duty on a barrel of white flour is at present about $ 1 and on a puncheon of cornmeal about $t 82, making the additional duties on thcso articles only 3 and 6 cents, and so on proportionally with regard to other articles or merchandize. During the discussion in the Colonial Council it has been observed, " that the reason why Government has not extended the dues in question on the imports, has been this, that by so doing it might give rise to smuggling but the conviction of the Colonial Council is, that so trifling an augmentation of the Customs-duos cannot have any influence in this direction, and smuggling will, under the auspices of vigilant custom-offlcers only be attempted at times with regard to a single article of insignificance, but not to any extent to create a loss so as to become a matter of any consideration. added, " on the import-duty," As the intention of the present draft is that of procuring increased revenues for the Land-treasury iu order to cover its present deficiency, the Colonial Council are of opinion, that there is special reason of taking this opportunity to make an addition to the provisions concerning the Absentee-tax to the Laud-treasury according to the ordinance of 19th February 1817, in order that this treasury may be secured against the increasing falling oft' of this revenue, which is caused thereby, that the courts have in some cases adopted this interpretation, that the said tax cannot be demanded from property under the administration of Executores testamenti or under other legal division of a succession in this island or in foreign parts, as long as the property has not been made over to the absent heirs, which interpretation is not in accordance with that contained in the former Hoard of Commerce's letter of 21st September 1824 ; and as the Land-treasury thereby loses a considerable revenue, the burthen on other tax-payers is at same time increased. The Colonial Council therefore propose, with 15 votes against 1, that the following provision be added as new paragraph 2 to the ordinance : " The Abseutee-tax imposed by the ordinance of 19 February 1817 shall in future also be levied on real property belougiug to estates of deceased persons, when the heirs are residing in foreign countries after the demise of the testator beyond the period mentioned in said ordinance, the right

of the mortgage holder however undisturbed. Should the testator die in foreign parts, the residence of the new owner in a foreign country shall in this respect be considered a continuation of that of the former proprietor. A Strange Mistake in an Omnibus. þÿ A lady who resides at Kensington, on returning by omnibus from town, missed her purse, which contained three or four pounds' worth of change. On relating her loss to her husband, with the conviction of having been robbed, he inquired who sat next to her in the omnibus ;

but being told that it was a very respectable and well-behaved gentleman, with a splendid ring on his finger, he advised his wife to see whether her purse might not have slipped into the lining of her dress instead of the pocket. This she did, when, lo ! there was found þÿ not the lady's purse þÿ but the identical splendid ring that had decorated the respectable gentleman's finger in the omnibus. Upon being taken to a jeweller to ascertain if it was a counterfeit, it proved to be worth £40.

Indicators of Earthquakes. þÿ The following extraordinary anecdote of the sensibility of cats to approaching danger from earthquakes is well authenticated In the year 1783, two cats belonging to a merchant of Messina, in Sicily, announced to him the approach of an earthquake. Before the first shock was felt, these two animals seemed anxiously to work their way through the door of a room in which they were. Their master observed their fruitless cllbrts, opened the door for them. At a second and third door, which they likewise found shut, they repeated their efforts, and on being set completely at liberty, they ran straight through the street, "and out of the gate ol the town. The merchant, whose curiosity was excited by this strange conduct of the cats, followed them into the fields, where he again saw them scratching and burrowing in the earth. Soon after, there was a violent shock of earthquake, and many of the houses of the city fell down, of which number the merchant's was one; so that he was indebted for bis lift to the singular foresight of his cats.

From the London Times. The following is from the pen of a person to whom we are often indebted for valuable information : þÿ "We are far from sharing the opinion of the German journals which imagine that a new Conference, held at Vienna, is on the point of concluding peace on the bases proposed in the letter of M. Drouyn de Lhuys to M. de Bourqueney. The demands of our Cabinet are certainly very moderate, too moderate even to secure guarantees for the future, and to satisfy the noble pride of the two great nations. But it should be first remarked that the letter of M. Drouyn de Lhuys, as well as the promises of the British Ministry, lay down as a principle that peace shall not be negotiated on the reestablisbment of the status quo; that the English and French people require a modification, both of diplomatic treaties ana of the Russian territory itself, and that portions of that territory are indispensable to insure the attainment of the different objects mentioned in the letter. It appears certain, moreover, that we have, at this very moment, undertaken the conquest of the Crimea, and we have reason to know that the allies intend to keep possession of Sebastopol, in order to guard in future against the preponderance of Russia in the Black Sea. On the other hand, it is indispensable, in order to secure to Germany the free navigation of the Danube, that Russia should cease to command the Sulina mouth of that river. Now, we are convinced that Russia will never consent to surrender either the Crimea or the Sulina, unless she is completely dis-

abled, and that it would be easier to reconquer onehalf of the empire than to obtain from her the cession of the smallest part of her dominions. There lies the insurmountable obstacle. The honour of the two nations, as well as of their Cabinets, is pledged to change the status quo, and the honour of Russia is pledged to maintain it. War, and a long war, is consequently inevitable. Independently of tnat material obstacle, wo anticipate others, resulting from the conventions to be entered into between the allies. Will Sebastopol bo kept by England, or by France ? Will that fortress be given to one, and Bomarsund to the other ? Those are serious questions, and the more we examine thom the more we remain convinced of the danger of a policy which obliges us to mount guard at the door of the Czar, to keep him under close arrest. But there is a much greater difficulty in the way of the ratification of the conditions proposed by M. Drouyn de Lhuys, namely, the opposition of the Ottoman Cabinet, which cannot really accept them. Before the war, and under the pressure exercised by Prince Menchikoff, the Divan had, it is true, offered to grant the five great Powers a certain right of protection over its Christian subjects. But the war has since annulled all the rights of protection formerly imposed by Russia, and the Porte, after its glorious victories, cannot alienate its sovereignty over the Principalities, or over the rayaha, in behalf of u collective or isolated protectorate. It

must be recollected that war has been undertaken, as M. Drouyn de Lhuys twice repeats in his letter, to maintain the integrity of the power of tho Sultan. Now, we should inflict upon it the most mortal blow if we were to confer on one or several foreign Sovereigns a right to interfere with the internal affairs of the nation. Would any Monarch in Europe submit to such vassalage ? What nation would not feel indig nant at it ? Turkey has certainly conquered a rank which authorizes her to be as proud as any other Power. As respects the free navigation of the Danube and the Straits, the Sultan, in virtue of the law of nations, has a right to refuse or grant a passage through them. It must also be observed that all stipulations to that effect are binding only in time of peace, and are set aside by war. It is consequently, evident that the portion of the Danube flowing through the Ottoman territory forms part of the empire, and that the Sultan may lawfully interdict its navigation, or subject it to certain duties. It would be strange indeed if the allies of the Sultan, who have allowed him to bear the brunt of the war, should conclude a peace at his expense and to the benefit of Germany, whose conduct has been hitherto so ambiguous, and who does not even appear disposed to declare war. We accordingly do not believe that the Porte, in justice to herself, can concede to any Power the protectorate of the Wallachian provinces or of its subjects, the free navigation of the Danube, or the free entrance into the Black Sea,

which, if granted to ships of war, would expose Constantinople to permanent danger. The allies will consequently be obliged to modify their pretensions. With respect to the anxious desire of Austriato secure the free navigation of the Danube, we see but one mode of accomplishing it þÿ that is by obtaining from Turkey the complete cession of the in Principalities, and compensating her for their loss another quarter ; and by wresting Bessarabia from Russia. All this is practicable ; but can only be achieved by an earnest and energetic war, and by curtailing the power of Russia." JStiaw From the Observer.

THE OBJECTS OF THE WAR. The objects of the war have now been so distinctly stated to the Russian Government, and Austria has so unequivocally expressed and recorded her assent to the the Emperor Nicholas propositions insisted on has by the Western Powers, that only left him to consider whether it is better to yield to such terms as these, or to prolong the contest. On the mere grounds of prudence and reason, it is probable that the political influence and the resources of the Russian empire would suffer less by accepting even these terms than by carrying on a struggle against all tho Great Powers, which can only terminate in greater sacrifices. But

3V» © IK © a K A 'T 'J 3. prudence and reason have had very little influence over the policy of the Emperor of Russia throughout these transactions, and he must still be regarded as the instrument of the passions he lias excited and the pride he has so bitterly wounded. He is called upon to give up all the privileges and treaties securing to Russia a protectorate over Moldavia, Wallachia, and Servia, some of which have existed since 1774 and 1779 þÿ open to the navigation of the Danube to its mouths, on the general principles established by the Congress of Vienna, and without distinction as to the territory through which the river þÿflows to consent to a revision of the convention of July, 1841, in the sense of a limitation of his own power in the Black Sea þÿ and, lastly, to renounce that protectorate of the Christians in Turkey, which formed the subject of the Menschikoff mission. Although these terms have our cordial concurrence þÿ and we think that less could not be asked to insure the object we have in view, which is not to injure or destroy the just rights of the Russian Government, but to prevent her power from being used to the detriment ana destruction of another state þÿ yet, in tho present relative position of the belligerent states, we can entertain no expectation that Russia will submit with sincerity and good faith to such propositions. Nor can we suppose that when the Austrian Government adopted these terms, and forwarded them to St. Petersburg, it expected that negotiations could now be

opened on such a basis. The question, however, remains up to this hour unsettled, what answer the Emperor Nicholas will give to such a communication, and what course Austria will pursue in the event of that answer being an unsatisfactory one ! At that point the diplomatic transactions which have so long kept the world in suspense, and possibly the war in abeyance, come to their natural termination ; and it is probable that this political decision will coincide in point of time with the operations which now give a more serious and decisive character to this contest. To the success of those operations, and to no other cause, we look for the ultimate restoration ot peace : and, although we have never held out the slightest expectation that thi3 war would be speedily or easily terminated, we are confident that the people of England will prolong for years their sacrifices and exertions, sooner than bate one jot of the rights they have undertaken to defend.

TURKISH ATTENTION to ENGLISHMEN On the morning of the 12th, Captain Maxwell, the correspondent of the Morning Chr»nicle, Mr. Hodgkins, the correspondent of the Daily news, and M. Hardtman, of the Kolner Zeitung, were arrested by the Wallachian militia, and taken to the police, who informed them that they must mtuin to llustchuk. The Belgian Consul, under whose protection British subjects still were on the 12th, proi against these proceedings, but in vain. The origin of this event is unknown, and it la therefore piemature to discuss it. It is po3jibie that Omar I'asha may have had some very imperative motive to justify his resorting to so arbitrary an act, and it is better to abstain from commenting upon it until that motive shall be known This much, however, is clear, that the gentlemen who have been thus treated, and the public at home, have a right to know what it was Unoffending Englishmen are not to be arrested and insulted with impunity ; and unless these correspondents and their companions committed, or were about to commit some offence. reparation is duo to them for the annoyance to which they have been exposed. Befoie England and France had declared themselves openly for Turkey, and when both were still vacillating, nothing could exceed the cordiality with which newspaper correspondents were received by the Tuiktsh Government and by Omar Pasha. ed more coolly, and this coolness became more frosty when roving jacks in office from England began to make their way up to Shumla " Lord de Ros, the Quartermaster-General," writes one of these gentlemen, " who makes no secret of his monomania on the subject of the press, did all in his power to prejudice Omar Pasha against us, he even implored him to send us away, and pointed out in a most feeling manner the prodigious evils that resulted from our presence These representations were hacked up by others who ought to have known better, and who, as Englishmen, ought to have been ashamed to talk thus to a foreigner of the greatest glory of their countiv þÿ the newspaper press. Definition of a Gentleman. The late and lamented Judge Talfourd, in the case of Wag vs. Kelson, tried at the Bristol, England, Assizes, shortly before his sudden death, thus defined the character of of a gentleman. The evidence proved that the defendant, while in the theatre, had said to the plaintiff, ' Do not speak to me, 1 am a gentleman, and you are a tradesman ' ' Gentleman,' said the learned judge, 'is a term which does not apply to any station, but to the mind and the feelings in every station. The man of rank who deports himself with dignity and candour, and the tradesman who discharges the duties of life with honor and integrity, are alike entitled to it ; nay the humblest artizan, who fulfils the obligation cast upon him wiih virtue and honor, is more entitled to the name of gentleman than the man who could indulge in offensive and ribald remarks, however big his station '

The "AVIS." Christiansted , Friday the 29 th September 1854. In our last number we published the Colonial Council's Report on the Draft of an Ordinance relative to the assessment of several taxes in this Island to the Land Treasury. To judge from the introductory remarks, which arc considered liberal, and the amendment to 1, which proposes an additional duty 3 per cent to be levied on im- of port duties, some inconsistency appears for it is clear and evident that an additional duty on the already exorbitant impost placed on the necessaries of life must be felt more oppressively by the poorer class, who would in this instance contribute the largest amount ol revenue, as they are generally the greater consumers. If an additional duty is laid on the luxuries of life, the weight would become less oppressive $ because those who chiefly indulge in them can well afford to pay additional duties, and thus perhaps would the object of the Ordinance be better realised. The high price and ly scarcity of provisions of war on account of the all sorts, like- in Europe, is very much felt at present, and we learn that some of those planters here, who formerly gave allowance to their laborers have now commenced to give them money instead ofallowance, as the latter is scarce and dear. We beg therefore to offer these remarks with the hope that, as taxes create privations in those who constitute the last term in the social series and who have 110 stock to raise, concessions and sacrifices will bo demanded of the rich.

(Fron the London Morning Herald.) The Suspicious Cruiser Grapeshot. It is stated that the Grapesliot, a vessel that created some stir by being reported some time since in the English Channel as a Yankee privateer, has " cleared out in a most mysterious manner from New Orleans, with a cargo of muskets." The New Orleans Delta of the 2nd inst. gives the following account of her : The Grapeshot, heavily armed, under Captain Baxter, cleared yesterday in a sudden and mysterious manner. She had been anchored off the mouth of the river for the last two months, during all of which time her acute and active captain lias been moving about oar city and neigbourhood in a manner to excite much curiosity and some alarm. One evidence of this was afforded by the Spanish consul, who dispatched a vessel and messenger to Cuba immediately on the arrival of the Grapeshot, and has made her the subject of several subsequent

ATI! 3, communications. We hear it whispered that a fast shcooner has already been chartered, by the same vigilant official, to proceed immediately to Havannah, to caution the authorities there to be on the look out for the Grapeshot. No doubt the said schooner will get there by the time the Grapeshot has made the circuit of the island, and accomplished her mission, which is doubtless one of immense importance to Cuba and the cause of freedom. There are others, however, who intimate lhatCaptain Baxter's sudden departure is connected with the arrival of the special Russian ambassador in New York. It is darkly hinted that so neat and fast-sailing a craft, so heavily armed, and commanded by so sturdy and determined a skipper, could never be intended for peaceable and commercial purposes. Why should not privateering be as honourable and profitable now as it was in 1814-15 and why is not the Russian as good a flag for that purpose as any other? On one point we feel pretty confident þÿ that there is not a vessel in the English or French service that could ever catch the Grapeshot, if she should show her heels to them, and not one of her size that would ever grapple with her in a fight. Those 35,000 muskets would be terribly effective in a close encounter. We cordially recommend her to the Emperor Nicholas's agent's favour as the very little saucy craft he requires; and, as for the muskets, we have the authority, of Major Kelly, who tried them in Cuba, for sayiug that they are good enough

for any. people who want to fight. But these are random ideas. We are utterly in the dark as to the design and movement of the Grapeshot, and content ourselves with announcing her departure, and the secession from a circle of adoring friends of her gallant and sonorous captain." Our cruisers in the West Indies will doubtless look after this " Grapeshot." Or is it necessary That the curtain should be drawn To save from further trouble The outside lookers-on ? " Is it any body's business. But the lady's, if her beau Rideth out with other ladies, And doesn't let her know? Is it any body's business, But rhe gentleman's, if she Should accept another escort, Where lie doesn't chance to he ? " If a person's on the side-walk, Whether great, or whether small, Is it any body's business Where that person means to call ? Or if you see a person While he's calling any where, Is it any o f your business What his business may be there? " The substance of our query, Simply stated, would be this: Is it any body's business What another's business is ? Whether 'tis, or whether 'tisn'f, We should really like to know, For we're certain, if it isn't, There arc some who make it so. " If it is, we'll join the rabble, And act the noble part Of the tattlers and defamers, Who throng the public mart : But if not, we'll act (lie teacher, Until each meddler learns, It were better, in the future, To mind his own concerns !"

Representation lo His Majesty. The accompanying draft of an ordinance laid before the Colonial Council in behalf of the St. Croix Burgher Council, regarding the raising of funds in favor of the St. Croix Land Treasury to defray the expenses connected with the importation of laborers from other places, has been a subject of very particular discussion in the Colonial Council, and in presenting the case for Your Majesty's most gracious decision, we beg leave most submissively to state as follows : þÿ 1, The number of laborers employed at the Sugar Cultivation of St. Croix, which constitutes the main, in fact the only source of revenue of the Island, was at the time of emancipation in 1848, in general sufficient, though with exceptions, but in the six years which have elapsed since that event, that number has decreased in an extraordinary degree, about to an amount of 25 per cent of the effective force of labor. This decrease has been effected not by emigration or any other general reduction of the population but by the country laborers removing to the towns, settling on so-called stock-estates, seeking employ -

drawing from labor on account of family relations, siddere og andre Indbyggere, som ikke ! and particularly by the rising generation being applied to other occupation than that of agriculture Be it observed that part of the population thus in the course of time leaving the sugar cultivation, generally speaking, that is to say with very rare exceptions have thereby attained positions not equally favorable as that of the country laborers. 2, In order to replace this decrease of laborers and moreover to rempdy the falling off of the average amount of daily labor caused by the excess of competition, the Planters have since emancipation made great exertions by procuring machinery, by augmenting their stock, and by altering the mode of cultivation, in many oases to an extent which the means at their disposal hardly warranted. þÿ Still with all these exertions on their part it has not been possible to prevent that already now several cane estates have been turned out of cultivation and that the same will have to be done on others, to the greatest detriment to the cultivation of the Island and to the ruin of the parties concerned, as of course also to the serious injury of the credit of the Island in general, We have here to observe, that all expenditure capital and all mechanical improve- of ments will not avail whenever the number of laborers required for the timely taking off of the crops and the proper attention to the fields in due Season is not secured, on the other hand the

abandonment of Estates and the corresponding increase of uncultivated tracts of land afford an opportunity and inducement for an increased number of individuals to seek their maintenance independently of the cane cultivation and thus it contains in itself the germ of the propagation of this evil. From all these causes it has become necessary to try to procure laborers from other places, just as, in general from similar reasons, has beon done in all those foroign Westindia Cowhich agriculture is still kept up 3, course of the last threo years attempts have been made by some of the Planters

and by several of them in conjunction (on the most favorable terms) to import laborers from diverse English Islands and from Madeira. These attempts (as well as correspondence carried on with an English mercantile establishment to procure an importation of laborers from China) have failed, because such undertakings can only be carried out on a larger scale, with means which far exceed what private individuals, particularly under the reduced circumstances of the Island, could possibly raise, partly also because emigrants, particularly from Madeira, are averse to enter engagements binding them to a certain property or to a certain employer, this not being made a condition for a free passage to the English Islands. As the English colonies, particularly Demerara, Trinidad and Jamaica, and, as far as we know, also the French Islands, besides pay out of the respective colonial Treasuries, which are assisted by the Mother Country with loans for this purpose, and in other manner a bonus of from $30 to $100 for each imported able laborer, they thereby offer greater guarantees to the undertakers and shipowners than could be secured by any private contracts. Credit-unious or the like establishments cannot be attained in St. Croix so long as a great number of the properties are very much incumbered and where not a few of those unencumbered are owned by proprietors in foreign countries; especially under relations that put it beyond any question that capitalists would vest money here,

and 6 bad crops having caused that there are no disposable means in the island itself. Here we must not lose sight of, that the poor crops in a great measure must bo attributed particularly to the want of labor. 4, The Colonial Council therefore agree with the Burgher Council on the desirableness or rather the urgency of effective measures being taken without delay for the importation of foreign laborers and cannot see, that this object could under existing circumstances be attained in any other manner, than the one proposed, viz : that the Landtreasury which we know for the present to be destitute of available means, should be authorised to take up a loan to be applied to this distinct purpose, under further directions and under public control. In as much as such an undertaking will entail an increase of taxes also upon those landed proprietors and other inhabitants, who most probably must be expected to require or to reap any immediate advantage from the importation of such laborers, the Colonial Council consider this course to be quite fair, as it is evident that the value of any property or of any business whatever in St. Croix depends upon the maintenance of the sugar cultivation and that without it the towns would soon be converted into fishing villages and the public institutions of the island, its judicial and schooling establishments would soon fall to the ground for want of revenues. As far as we know, the correctness of these views, according to which under the practical circumstan-

ces, the whole island ought to contribute, has never been called in question in any of those Westindia Islands, which, their exertions in the abovenamed direction being vigorously encouraged and assisted by the respective Governments, have ultimately recovered from positions which were even more critical and dangerous than the one in which St. Croix is actually placed. 5, We think it proper, to observe, that the island of St. Croix, precisely on account of the serious diminution of the force of labor and of the production, which has taken place since emancipation, hardly can hope ever to obtain a loan in any way sufficient for the purpose in question, be it even on burdensome terms, without public guarantee. We must however be of opinion, that the island is entitled to the assistance of the State Treasury iu a case like the present, and the more so as there not here as elsewhere

3 JN <0 m © a X A T U 3 in similar eases þÿ whilst the compensation, so late in time and so inadequate in amount as it was, only in part came to the actual owners of landed property þÿ has been done anything on the part of the State to uphold the cultivation of the island and its credit after so severe a convulsion, though in Denmark also the justice and policy of special arrangements tending thereto, have been acknowledged and urged in the earlier part of the discussions, even to the extent of disregarding the right of the individual to compensation. The later laws on Customs, especially the almost total repeal of the benefit of the previously existing reduced duty on rum, and the late repeal of the remission of 25 per cent on the import duty hitherto allowed, which de facto was to the advantage of all sugars exported from St. Croix to Denmark, and iu regard of which the Planters, on account of the great demand for ship-room, have not indirectly received any remuneration, have placed the production of the island even in a less favorable position than heretofore. OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL Second Session Representation to His Wajcsty. (Continued ) In regard to the special enactments of the draft we beg leave to observe : ad 1. The proposed amount of $60,000 would be ample in case we could hope to procure a somewhat sufficient number of laborers from the smaller English or from the Canary Islands, the cost of each not to exceed $40 or 50, but there is from several causes but little prospect of obtaining from them, as the laborers on the former are certainly more disinclined to work than any in the Danish Islands, and would under no conditions bind themselves to remain here as laborers for any specified length of time ; the latter have not proved particularly adapted or disposed to continuous field labor. The English Colonies, Cuba and Portorico therefore prefer now, without regard to the great outlay, to import Chinese, engaged for 5 or 7 years (and without obligation to defray their return voyage) ; these must, according to the numerous and detailed elucidations, official as well as private, which are before the Council, be considered as physically well adapted and also as more willing and industrious than any other known class of such laborers in the tropical climates. They can however not be obtained in smaller numbers than cargoes of about 300 in one transport and at a cost for each individual landed in the West Indies of $100 or, on account of the present amount of freights, something more ; at the same time it is a fact, that well known English undertakers, who are versed in such transac-

tions, are willing to import Chinese laborers to this Island, provided their expenses and commission be guaranteed. The proposed amount would thus, in as far as Chinese are exclusively meant, to procure to the Island an additional force of between 500 and 600 laborers of the best quality for a time of, until further, 5 years, and we entertain no doubt, that even such an addition would materially contribute to enable the planters to counteract the efforts of the present want of laborers, and very likely also to keep up the newly formed connection without any additional burden to the state. We can therefore not recommend any reduction of the above stated amount, which, considering that it must not be exhausted in the first year, must be looked upon as a minimum. It would probably not bo advisable to fix the rate of interest in the law at 6 per cent as a maximum, a private loan to the Land Treasury especially could not bo obtained under such conditions. ad 2. The tax proposed under Litra a of 10 cts. pr: An: for each acre of estates land in St. Croix, the soil may be cultivated or not, we look upon as proper and not unfair, if a clause be added in regard to such land, which can be proved to be of no use or render any revenue whatever

AVI® to the owners. According to the annexed lists of all the landed properties in St. Croix the area of the same amounts to about 51,170 Acres, of : which c: 19,450 acres are stated to be in cane cultivation, c: 26,000 applied to other use and barren ( therefore not taxed) land c: 5,000 Acres. Thus there are about 45,000 Acres, which at the rate of the proposed tax of 10 cents would yield $4,500 p: A:, or somewhat more in case land not used by any one, but still fit for use, be subjected to the law. It must however be observed, that a very considerable proportion of this area pays no tax whatever to the Land Treasury, as besides the so called Cavalry and Artillery Tax, which is exclusively paid by the Sugar Estates, a Ground Tax (New Tax,) of 16 cents per Acre is likewise exclusively paid by the land in cane cultivation, the rest, comprising the entire area of the Stock Estates pays the Ground Tax to the State Treasury with 21J cents per acre, but nothing to the Land Treasury, and it is our firm conviction, that there is not alone no objections to impose a tax as the one in question upon such lands, but also that the position of the Stock Estates and the chances of a profitable use of their soil have since emancipation improved to such a degree, that the State and particularly the Land Treasury, even without reference to this present matter, can with fairness demand of them a moderate contribution to the general wants of the Island. The cause of this change must be mainly sought in the cir-

cumstance, that whilst by far the greater number of such properties in a series of years previous to emancipation were made but little use of on account of want of hands (the proprietors in many cases being unable to procure the necessary number of slaves, as their work was looked upon as | more lucrative on Sugar Estates, and the latter were in possession of greater means to rear stock and make extra revenues by the sale of grass, wood, lime eto:) þÿ the stock estates now offer to the laborer equally good (and with regard to their personal position þÿ the want of control over the work and the time of working) in many cases a more attractive condition ; the rise in the value of such land is therefore manifested not only by some single sales, but also by the now beginning division of it and the dwellings erected thereon, particularly by former estate laborers. It would principally be some few Sugar Estates, having extensive and little productive tracts of pasture or hill land, that could consider themselves overburthened by such an addition to their already immoderate taxes; wc are however of opinion, that any owner of such estates would cheerfully consent to boar also this burden, in case at the same time an addition to the number of laborers be ensured. The tax proposed under letter b, of 64 cents per month is intended to be paid by the person who employs such a laborer imported for account of the Land Treasury (or eventually, should he under a future development of the relations of

labor obtain permission to work for his own account by the laborer himself). We opine at the same time, that there is all reason to demand of the proprietor who first employs such a laborer for any length of time, an adequate contribution to the Land Treasury, supposing the contracts to have a duration of an amount, of $10, and with a shorter duration of the contract, in proportion, of which amount in case such a laborer should remove to another estate previous to the expiration of the contract (which removals ought not to meet with too groat difficulties), the new employer would have to refund a fair proportion Thereby supporting an immigration of at least 500 Chinese to bo effected within the first two years, an additional contribution would be raised to the payment of the first outlay and interest of $5,000 For general information wo remark furthermore, that a part of the first outlay consists in advances to the immigrants, which will hardly amount to

more than $10 for each, which is usually stipulated to be paid back by monthly deduction from their wages. ad 4. The Council are aware of no objection that would be made against this enactment, but look upon it as desirable that there be added an express declaration authorizing the Government to lay down the necessary legal rules as well in regard to immigration as also in regard to the general position and the specific legal interests of the laborers imported partly or entirely for public account, which, as long as the whole undertaking is new here, could be settled by provisional laws or regulations. The existing local labor regulations could in general not be applicable to relations and contracts which must be regulated by the conditions which arc granted in foreign places. We take this opportunity to point out, that the uniform payment <$-c., for the estate-laborers in St. Croix fixed by the labor-regulations (which provisions however from what has been elucidated by no means prevent these that are willing to take task-work from earning more) merely exists in consequence of the want of the necessary number of laborers for the cultivation of the island ; naturally at a sacrifice to those estates, the greater resources of which would otherwise enable them, by increasing the wages already established, to attract laborers from estates of less resources. The readers of the Tidende already know that Councillor C. F. Ohsten, Intendant of His þÿMajesty s Royal Customs in this Island, proceeds in a few days to Denmark. Much of that þÿgentleman s time has of late been engaged in remodelling the þÿCustom s Laws of this place, the Draft of which it was our peculiar advan- j tage, through the medium of a friend, to peruse many months ago. Averse to bestowing praise where it may easily be construed into flattery, we nevertheless must say that we were highly j instructed, interested, and edified at the amount | of information the Draft placed before us, and convinced us of the positive knowledge Councillor Ohsten had secured himself with, respecting the nature, character and resources of our commerce, and the points on which its prosperity depends. Therein we found minutely detailed what is the amount of our commerce with Denmark, England, Spain, Germany, France, Italy, and other European nations, and what could, by changes in the duties and imposts in this island, tend to enlarge and advance that commerce. Next followed in equal detail the nature and amount of the trade of this Island ' with the United States, both North and South | Then the British North American Provinces ; Venezuela, New Granada, þÿ C., in South America. Lastly, the Inter-colonial trades, to which diverge, the imported Merchandize, to wit, Porto Rico, Cuba, St. Domingo, Hayti, Curacao, <5'c-i to leeward, and St. Croix, and the English and French Islands to windward. This Draft, mo-

delled by Councillor Ohsten. was submitted by the Government, to the Colonial Council at its last session, and we believe has since been published in tho St. Croix Avis. Time, however, has not allowed us to examine whether the original Draft perused by us underwent any change ; as it passed through the Colonial Council, but wo are of opinion it has not, excepting may-be in one or two items of little or no moment. As the Draft, after passing the Colonial Council, and as it now stands, must receive the supervision and signature of His Majesty, in order to become the Law of this Island, Councillor Oiisten, wishing to accelerate it, and in order to elucidate points, by personal explanation, that would otherwise require time for consideration, has obtained J from Government leave of absence, to assist at home with the Draft, which must be taken as the result of his labor, and establishes in his favor the interest he manifests in all things calculated to add and improve the condition and prosperity of these Islands. Councillor Ohsten is an Oflicial of the liberal type, and is often found standing between old degenerated Laws and worn out systems, and would like to impart a little fresh blood into the body politic of these Islands. Councillor Ohsten may be assured that he enjoys the confidence and good wishes of a large portion of this community.

From Bell's Weekly Messenger, August 26 Affecting anecdote of the late Captain Packer. We find in a letter from the Black 8ea, a delightful trait of humanity and benevolence, in the midst of the horrors of war : þÿ þÿ Captain þÿBarker sloss is severely felt by the officers of the Firebrand, and by all who, knowing him, could appreciate his public and private life. You will have heard of the circumstance connected with his þÿship f s iist visit to Kostendje, some four months ago, from w hich place some Cossacks had just retreated, leaving behind many proofs of their amiability of disp osition. In one hut were found the bodies of a Bulgarian man and woman, upon whose remains was stretched a child but a few months old ; its hand was extended upon its þÿmother b s reast, and through a part of his little wrist the ball had passed which had deprived her of life; near them was a little terrorstricken boy, about three years old, whose left arm was in a sad state from the effects of no less than five bullet wounds, immediately on their discovery, the two boys were sent on board the Firebrand and properly cared for, Captain Barker expressing his intention of taking them entirely under his charge. These little fellows arc still in the Firebrand, where, of course, among sailors, they find an abundance of nurses. The eldest, a fine little intelligent Bulgarian specimen, answers to the name of þÿ Johnny þÿFirebrand, and already speaks English ; his brother has just been weaned, by tho assistance of a goal, and is at present undergoing the painful mysteries of

teething, having thereby imparted great knowledge to the unmarried officers of the ship on that subject. When the time arrives for the Firebrand to be paid off the officers will be disposed, and there will be no home for these voong Bulgarians. There is to be. 1 believe, a subscription in the fleet, on their behalf, and I am quite sure that this will not be limited to us ol the Black Sea, and that there will also be found some English charities whose funds are applicable to such a þÿcase.

A discovery, which is likely to be of great advantage to agriculture, has just been reported to the Agricultural Society of Clermont (Oise). A gardener, whose frames and hothouse required painting, decided on making them black, as likely to attract the heal better, and from a principle of economy he made use of gas tar instead of black paint. The work was performed during the winter, and on the approach of spring the gardener was surprised to find that all the spiders and insects which usually infested his hot-house had disappeared, and also that a vine, which for the last two years had so fallen off that he had intended to replace it by another, had acquired fresh force and vigour, and gave every sign of producing a large crop of grapes. He afterwards used the same substance to the posts and trellisworks which supported tho trees in the open air, and met with tho same result, all the caterpillars and other insects completely disappearing. It is said that similar experiments have been made in some of the vineyards of the Gironde with similar results, þÿ Galignani.

From the Observer, September 10, 1854. Denmark. þÿ The great meeting of merchants, bankers, and the trading classes, convened by the Society for Upholding the Popular Constitution of 1849, took place in the Casino, at Copenhagen, on the 29th ult. The Casino, capable of accomi modating 3000 persons, was crowded, and the assembly would have been much greater but for the Government prohibition of open-air meetings. The chair was taken by Mr. C. E Fenzer, formerly one of the representatives of Copenhagen in Parliament, and among the speakers were Mr. C. E. Broberg, merchant, and also a member for Copenhagen; M. AVessely, a senator; H. P. Hansen, banker ; J. C Jacobsen, a brewer, and member of Parliament ; F. Barfod, a member of Parliament; M. Hammarish, a professor; D. B. Adler and M. Dauchell, merchants ; and Mr. K. Puggaard, of the firm of Puggaard and Co. The commercial and moneyed classes were never before so fully represented in any public meeting in the capital of Denmark. Mr. Broberg, who proposed the fourth resolution, warned the meeting that it implied their readiness to stand upon an impeachment of the ministry, and the refusal of taxes, should such an extreme become necessary ; but it was adopted with enthusiasm. A large sum was raised as the first portion of a fund þÿ for supporting the patriots dismissed from office by a tyrannical cabinet for their votes in Parliament, and for the assistance of the national press against illegal and ruinous þÿprosecutions. Mr. Adler, who proposed it, gave a thousand Danish dollars.

The visit of Punce Albert to the Emperor of the French, to be present at the Review of the Troops encamped at Boulogne, in sight | of the shores of Great Britain, is a compliment well-desoi ved by the Sovereign and the People who are our most faithful Allies The Consort of the Queen of England does not proceed on any mere political mission. He is not entrusted with any formal Diplomatic functions, lie will be accompanied by no Civil Dignntaries whatever. Hisenj tourage will be altogether Military. But it will be in every wav worthy of the Great Sovereign with whom he is so intimately connected, the country from which ho proceeds, and the Nation which is prepared to receive him with all cordiality and distinction. Field-Marshal of the British Army. Prince Albert will appear with a military prestige becoming his high rank, and not unworthy of a prominent positional the great military spectacle of our gallant Allies We are not famous for great military gatherings in England ; but when the Consort of our Sovereign confers the dignity of his presence, and the practical mark of his countenance, upon this great neighbouring display, it is right that the compliment should be suitable and completo. The Prince will be attended to the field by a numerous staff, by the mount-

ed orderlies of the þÿQueen Guards, s and some of the highest officers of the British Army including the Commander-in-chiefþÿ will be present on this interesting and important occasion. For important it must still be called not as the commencement only, or rather the outward confirmation, of great events undertaken in conceit by the great nations, hut us affording not merely a common source of gratification to the people of France and Englnnd, hut holding out to wavering or hostile Powers the strongest and most obvious evidence of the entire cordiality and unbroken good faith which marks the course of the Allies in all their combined prooceedings in defence of the great principles of justice and of civilisation. The two Constitutional Monarchs of Belgium and of Portugal will be also present. And although, as we before observed, no formal political movement is intended, or even indicated, it will be impossible for þÿmen s minds not to dwell upon the union and the power that will be here displayed. Even the King of Prussia himself þÿ with all his armed population þÿ may look and pause over this armed friendly meeting, lie may perhaps reflect that all Ins admiring visions must not be ditected to the North, whilst scenes are passing iri the South and West, not altogether unworthy of his observation. He must cast an eye betimes upon the Rhine, and not direct his contemplations exclusivelv to the Vistula or the Wolga. But let feeble or fainthearted politicians look as they may, vve cannot but hope that

the scenes of Tuesday and of Wednesday next þÿ in the open sight of France and England þÿ will be of present good augury, and of future brilliant hopes of many a year of united triumphs in War, and of continued cordiality in Peace. Prince Albert will take bis departure fiom Osborne House to-moriow in the Royal Yacht of our beloved Sovereign, and proceed up Channel for Boulogne, where he will disembark at an early hour on Thursday morning. His Royal Highness will be accompanied þÿ in addition to his own suit þÿ by the Duke of Newcastle, her þÿMajesty sMinister for War, and will be attended to the French port bv four vessels of war of the Royal Navy. The attendants and horses, &c , have already proceeded to France. The Royal and distinguished visitors of the French Emperor will witness the grand military evolutions of the camp on Tuesday and Wednesday next, and lake their departure on Thursday. The camp is now composed of about 100,000 men. and presents a most imposing and brilliant appearance. þÿ lb. September 3.

A public writer, describing the Russian prisoners brought from Bomarsund te Shcerness, ex- J presses an opinion that such men, thin, lathy, and unintelligent looking, cannot be expected ultimately to resist the superior soldiers of Western Europe. A little reflection will show how groundless such opinions are, and how dangerous.

<e R <D 1£ 31 ATI 3, We arc told that if we saw our Guards and other , choice regiments, after a few weeks suffering at Varna, we could not suppose that in their emaciated, feeble, and dejected condition, they were the same men who left our shores in the pride and strength of health and of hopeful anticipations. If we apply this to the Russian and Finnish soldiers who spent the whole of last winter in garrison duty under the severe climate of Aland, and when spring returned were prevented by our fleets from receiving that relief and comfort which they so much required, and naturally expected, we ought not to look with contempt on such enemies. Of the Russians who triumphantly followed the older Napoleon from Moscow to Paris, nearly 200,000 men of all arms, from the Imperial Guards even to the hideous Kalmuck, all were well-grown men, capable of fatigue and endurance, though their infantry had a complicated, clumsy routine of manual exercise, and their dirty habits were calculated to engender putrid fevers and other fatal complaints. Their encampments, surrounded by heaps of the offal of slaughtered animals þÿ

the intestines and the heads (which they do not eat,), smelt like hot-beds of contagion, enough to kill our well-fed Grenadiers in a few hours. 3 From the St. Thomas Times, October 18. TIIK WUATIIER. The Weather for three days past has been unparalleled in the experience of the oldest inhabitants. On Sunday the Sun scarce shown out, and it rained during the entire night. Monday morning the Barometer had fallen three lines, and has continued so until now, occasionally rising a-tenth, and again falling to a fixed point. During all Monday the wind blew strongly from the South, and at times South-West ; this, as all who are acquainted with our harbour well know, raised an immense swell, and cautioned all ships in port to be alive to the benefits of good chains and anchors. The several vessels-of-war in port, viz., Danish corvette Najaden, English steamer Devastation, English Brig Mariner, and French steamer L'Ardent, lowered their light spars, and otherwise prepared themselves for the event of approaching bad weather. The 11. M. S Wye, lying at the quarantine ground, was rather dangerously exposed during the whole period ; she lay at the mouth of the hat bout, and being light from want of coal, tossed and labored a good deal. She is said to have lost an anchor, and yesterday morning was ultimately forced to leave the quarantine and come into harbour. The other mail steamers, comprising the Atrato, coaling for Europe, the Dee and Teviot, kept up constant steam, lest they may have been forced to go to sea, and so avoid danger. The Solent and Eagle, which are undergoing repairs, and have a portion of their machinery out, were obliged to trust to the power of their chains and anchors þÿ which,

we are confident, are all-sufficient for an emergency. All the merchant vessels, square rigged, schooners. <J-c , although at times in thteatening positions, have successfully ridden out the storm in safety, and excepting the wharves, and a half dozen lighters, the harbour has escaped with little or no injury. The Town, however, presents a very different spectacle, for although the houses have not received material injury, the rain, which may be said to have lasted for a period of sixty consecutive hours, has caused our hills to convert their ruts into rapids, and flooded the whole of our principal streets, tearing up gutters, and carrying away bridges, and entering several houses, and some of our principal stores along the main street. Among these disasters it is our melancholy duty to record the loss of life, numbering some say to four, others three, while we are positively certain of two men þÿ one aged, and another iri the prime of life. It is not possible to ascertain correctly by what means those poor creatures have arrived at so untimely an end, but we must conjecture that in the dark they lost their path and foot hold, and the impetuosity of the gutters must have hurled them onwards, and made them unconscious, together no doubt with the bruises from stones and branches of trees, life was soon extinct. We witnessed one body as it lay with the legs wrapped around the trunk of a tree in the market place, and the sight was indeed appalling. For the cause of humanity let us

hope that the vital spark in this poor creature had fled long ere its sufferings arrived at that termination. The weight of water that has fallen in this Island within three days may be conceived when, as far as the best judgment can go, thirty-two lines have been caught in the rain-guage, adequate to what in ordinary periods would fall in six months. The stagnation which it causes to all business transactions and trades is scarcely explained. The inconvenience to the commercial community in particular has been sorely tested, as the weather has occurred at a time when a mail was about to depart for Europe. Candles and lamps in the counting rooms had in consequence to be resorted to. All out-door trades have of course been suspended, and butchers' meat, milk, &c , could not be had at a premium. Our Wednesday's paper appears beyond the time, as we could not in a dark office with wet types, and a storm outside, proceed leisurely to wotk. Three days of labor have been lost in the office : but with

iiT!I . now activity the goes to press. of half-a-dozen hands our paper Cane cultivation in this Island being all but extinct, we have not been alarmed for the loss of crops in the country ; however, those few estntes in the levels. Musquito Bay for example, that had some fields in cultivation, are now so completely inundated that the caries will rot before they can be taken from off the ground. There has nevertheless been considerable loss in Cattle, Mules, Horses, See... on the several estates. The roads on the hill sides are represented to be in a deplorable state þÿ chasms torn across them so large as to defy bringing to town any Milk, Wood, Vegetables, or other articles for town consumption. The following is the proclamation of Marshal St.Arnaud to the French troops, which is said to have produced an excellent impression: þÿ "Soldiers ! You have given a noble example of perseverance, calmness, and energy, in the midst of painful circumstances, which must be forgotten. The hour has come to combat and to conquer "The enemy has not awaited us on the banks of the Danube. His armies, demoralised and destroyed by disease, are retiring with difficulty, and Providence has, perhaps, spared us the trial of those unhealthy regions. It is Providence which now calls us to the Crimea, a healthy country like your own, and to Sebastopol, the seat of Russian power in these seas, where we. go to seek the guarantee of peace and of a return to our hearths. "This enterprise is grand, and worthy of you. We will realise it with the aid of the most formidable military and naval preparations that were ever seen. þÿ The allied fleets, with 3.0(K) guns and their 25,000 brave sailors, your emulators and companions in arms, will carry to the Crimea a British army whose great valor your fathers learnt to respect, a chosen division of those Ottoman soldiers who have just proved their valour before your eyes, and a French force, which I have the right and am proud to call the elite of all our army. "1 see there more than a guarantee for success þÿ I see success itself. Generals, colonels, and officers of all ranks, and all armies, you will participate and instil into the spirit of your soldiers the con-

fidence that inspires mine. We will soon salute the three flags united and flying from the ramparts of Sehastopol, with our natural cry of 'Vive I'Empereur !' "The. Marshal Conunander-in- Chief, St. Arnaud. "Head-quarters, Varna, August 25."

It says þÿ of a rotary machine for improving the " We mentioned some time ago the departure of Mr. Titus Lespes for France, the first by whom the Turbine was introduced in our colony ; and we stated that he went in quest of instruments for the improvement of our manufactures. We are happy to be enabled now to announce that Mr. Titus Lespes's efforts in France have been crowned with full success. He has, conjointly with a distinguished engineer, Mr. Coster, patented his invention of a new Turbine or rotary machine, which he calls Purgeur a mouvements differentiels ; and it appears that this instrument is calculated to effect a veritable revolution upon our sugars of inferior quality. It was tried in Paris at the establishment of Mr. Coster, before an assemblage of colonial planters and others, amongst whom were Messrs. do Perrinelle, Lechevalier, Bornhave, Crassous, Fougainville, Louis Levassor, &.C., and the results obtained were as follows: þÿ The sugar placed in the Turbine was of a quality quoted at 2 francs below what is usually designated bonne quatrieme; and yet, after five minutes of rotation the instrument gave it a quality which was valued by those present at 8 francs above the bonne quatrieme; this was accomplished, too, in half the time usually taken by the old rotary engines. We have been assured that this Purgeur a mouvements differentiel costs but half the price of the turbines of Cail ; and that

it requires, in any motive power whatsoever, not more than the force of two men to set it in operation. Rem a kk a hi. h Cure of Cholera. þÿ The Gazette dts Hopitaux, of the 19th publishes a remarkable cure of cholera by mistake. Dr. Roger (de I'Ore) having been called upon to visit a patient in the worst stage of cholera, prescribed, but with scarcely the slightest hope that it would be efficacious, an emetic of 1J gramme of ipecacuanha, to be taken in three doses (prises) at intervals of halfan-hour. The person who was charged to administer the ipecacuanha, seeing the word prises, and finding that the medicine was a powder, imagined that it was a kind of snuff, and that three prises meant three pinches. He consequently made the patient stuff up a third. The ipecacuanha thus administered, instead of making the patient vomit, caused him to sneeze with such force, and for so long a time, that it violent reaction took place. Heat returned to the surface, all the symptoms of cholera ceased, and when the physician paid his next visit he found his patient cured. þÿ Galignani.
