From t he Observer, September 24, 1854. End of t lie Expedition to the BALTIC.

The return of a portion of the forces from the Baltic, and the tenor of Sir Charles Napier's last despatches, indicate the termination of the present naval campaign in the north of Europe. It must be acknowledged that the results of these operations fall much below what was expected from the gigantic naval armament which sailed a few months ago from the Downs. There is an obvious disproportion between preparations of such magnitude and the effects produced by them upon the power of the enemy ; and, with a view to the more efficient conduct of the next campaign, even more than for the purpose of unavailing recrimination, it is desirable that the causes of this disappointment should be fully considered and understood. Mistakes have, of course, been committed þÿ some from want of knowledge, some from want of judgment, and some from want of resolution ; but, on the other hand, an amount of experience has been gained in this peculiar warfare which ought to render the recurrence of such blunders impossible another year. It is to be regretted that by far the more powerful of our two great fleets, especially in steatn I þÿine of-battie ships has been employed throughout the summer where there was least work to be performed. The allied powers had two objects to accomplish in the Baltic. The first was to shut up the whole naval power of Russia, to prevent every vessel of war from leaving Iter ports, or to give battle to the Russian fleet with success if her 18 þÿline þÿof battle ships

ventured beyond the shelter of her land batteries. The second was to blockade and threaten her coasts, and to attack and destroy her fortifications wherever they were thought to be assailable by naval artillery. The first of these objects has been completely, and the second partially, effected ; but the question is whether the Admiralty exercised a sound judgment in the means they employed. For the sole purpose of obtaining the mastery of the Baltic, and of fighting the Russian fleet if it came out, the armament appears to have been greater than was requisite ; and while it contained several first-class ships, such as the Duke of Wellington, the St. Jean d'Acre, j and the Neptune, which could scarcely be brought through the Bell from their draught | of water, and were ill adapted to such a navigation, there was a strange and lamentable deficiency in steamers of light draught, such as those which have been constructed within the last few weeks, when it is too late to use I them. The naval department of the Admi- ) rally performed its duty to perfection in send ing to sea the vessels which were ordered for commission ; but so much cannot be said for the political and strategical ability shown in the direction and use of these gigantic weapons. It is due to Sir Charles Napier to add, j that before the commencement of the war, and before his own appointment to the com- ; mand of the fleet, he had strongly urged upon j the Admiralty the necessity of providing steam gunboats in iarge numbers ; and that !

upon taking the command he also desired j that a division of troops should embaik with the expedition. Yet the gunboats were not prepared, and the French division of troops had to be sent out in supplementary ships in the month of August. The result has shown that Bomarsund could as well have been taken by 4,000 men and the marines and j seamen of the fleet as by the 12 000 who ! were afterwards sent there. A more serious charge against the Ministers of the Crown who are responsible for the direction of the war is that they appear to have sent the fleet to sea without any deliberate plan of campaign. They armed a very powerful squadron, they placed in command of it an officer who had a great reputation for skill nnd daring, and they left him to make the best use he could of iiis forces. Until the attack on Bomarsund was resolved upon and gallantly executed. Sir Charles Napier seems to have had little notion of

B »» © US '6 !t 2S ATII3. systematic operations. In particular, no serious attempt was made to bring the Russian fortresses in the Baltic to the test of a severe naval cannonade. The first attacks on Bo marsutid and on Hango Udd or Gustafsvarn, in the month of June, were bombardments by the steamers throwing hollow shot at a long range, which could produce no effect on the solid walls. In attacking places fortified with stone facings, the fire which is harmless at 1,000 yards becomes destructive at 500, and would be irresistible at 150, If there be water to float a ship within a very short range of the enemy's batteries, it is probable that the nearer she approached the less she would suffer, and the shorter would be the contest. At Sweaborg, I he hatleiies are principally hewn in the solid rock, and are therefore unassailable in front ; but at Cron stadt or Mango the experiment should have been tried. The Russians themselves have shown their own opinion by blowing up Gus tafsvarn as soon as the fall of Bomaisund was known. A combined attack on a for tress of the first class, such as Cron6tadt undoubtedly is, demands extensive preparations and great forethought in the Government at home, to be guided in the hour of action by military genius. The attack on Copenhagen succeeded because Nelson refused to see t he signal of bis superior officer ordering him to retreat, and it is in that dauntless spirit that the trophies of the British navy have been won. The great difficulty our fleet has had to encounter during this summer is that of the

navigation of the Baltic, and it is impossible to speak too highly of the manner in which this obstacle has been surmounted The lighthouses were extinguished, the buoys and landmaiks removed, the charts are imperfect, and the charmelsand currents scarcely known. In case of rough weather, the large ships have no port to run to foi shelter, and no searoom to enable them to weather the gale Yet (Up to the present time no serious acc.i dent has occurred. In former expeditions to the Baltic, ail the ships selected for that service were of the rank of our old seventy fours, not equal to a first class fiigate of the present day, and no doubt when the results of this year's experience are collected, it will be found that the second and third rate ships are better adapted for these operations than the first rates The naval departments of England and France should, therefore, proceed unremittingly to consider and prepare for more regular operations in the Baltic than those of the past season. At Sebastnpol we may destroy the influence of Russia over the E'isi ; but, unless that blow should reduce the Emperor Nicholas to ask for terms, it is only by opening the road to St. I'eteisburg that we can reckon on dictating a secure nnd honourable peace. Cronstadt once taken and destroyed, the capital of the northern empire is lor the future without defence against the maritime Powers, and the fear of such a catastrophe is more likelv ihan any oihei means to secure our triumph

The "AVIS." Christiansted, Friday the 27 th October 1854. We alluded to the proposed dismemberment of the Upper Court in a former number ; but in a very cursory manner. The subject is of too vast importance to pass over without comment ; and t lie remarks we now offer may go some way to convince illiberal and narrow-minded persons, that if the proposed method be adopted, the Colonics will inevitably be deprived of one of its brightest institutions. If as a Court of Appeal the Upper Court be composed of one Chief Judge, instead of three, as it is at present, what better guarantee and greater security will be realised ? In the Lower Court there is but one Judge, who pronounces judgments. If these judgments are appealed to the Upper Court, and that is also composed of one Judge only, are better results expected than from the Court of three members? The difference in judgments pronounced respectively in the Lower and Upper Courts arises from the different view which each Judge takes of the case. And this difference of view is the natural result arising from man's liability to err, which is certainly more evident where one mind is employed than where two or more are. Let a Judge be of the most conscientious character, he cannot prevent his affections or his own interests from influencing his judgment. Let for example a case, the result of which must greatly concern the individual interest of a man, be brought before him for his judgment, which judgment is to settle the case for ever, does not his interests act powerfully in warping his

judgment ? Is it easy for a man's understanding to act uninfluenced by his will? We think not. But Brutus, it might be said, sat in judgment on his own sons, and there are other men as conscientious as Brutus. True, hut the very rareness of such cases is the very reason why they are held up to admiration. If it were a common occurrence there would be no necessity of publishing such conduct to the world. "Self-love" says Locke, "will make men partial to themselves and friends," andthiswesay that where a judgment pronounced is the result of the combined opinions of three, we are less liable to have a partial judgment ; for it would be rare indeed that the interests or self-love of every one of these three were dependent on the result of their judgment. Humanuin est crrnre" is a truth which should never be left out of mind, when we would frame institutions to which we sult thereof, justice. must look for impartiality and as a re- " Two heads are better than one," in this as in most cases, and our fellow-colonists will learn have like Aesop's dog grasped at the to their sorrow, that in this case we " shadow and lost the substance." The matter has been viewed by some from a pecuniary point of view ; but, not to say more on this subject, we may add that this retrenchment in the judiciary establishment of this Island, and the incorporation of offices, one into another, which is not of rare occurrence, must at no very distant period deprive the Colonies of efficient

® » (0 a X A ? 2 3, functionaries. Judging from the fact, that in this Island there are at present but five lawyers, some of whom are on the eve of leaving, and other two are acting Policemasters, without any hope of seeing any more among us, we may justly say, that the means of obtaining justice appears to be decidedly on the ebb.

From the St. Thomas Times, October 21. THE WEATHER ! A private letter front St. John's informs us that it had rained in that Island from Sunday morning, the 15th, to Thursday morning, the 19th. At Cruz Bay 34 inches of water had fallen, and in other tarts of the Island even that quantity had been exceeded. No mention is however made whether much injury has been sustained by this unusual fall of rain. We must, nevertheless, suppose that some damage has accrued, if only from the immensity of wash that took place as the water rushed to the sea shore. St. John's is still infinitely more agricultural than we are,

In our last number speaking of the rainguage, we used the term lines, þÿ wo beliovc among practical men, this is understood to imply inches Theoretically we know a line signifies the 10th or 12th part of an inch, as one or the other of the nations might use it þÿ (Fd

and the soil as a consequence is what those interested in the Island bestow their united attentions upon, and in this view we are to comprehend that the rain renders more injury in proportion to St. John's than to ourselves. In oar town, the Police, attended by a large staff of laborers, carts and cartmen, are engaged in emptying the gutters of the immense quantity of ground lodged in them by the heavy rains, as well as that which lies heaped up along the main street. This labour, as no doubt our readers might perceive, becomes rather annual now, for scarce a year passes over hut the principal gutters become choked at the bridges, and overflows the water into the streets; not unfrcquently doing damage to the stores. In view of this we should say that it is worthy the observation of some of our Architects and Civil Engineers to ascertain whether a description of bridges could not be planned to insure sufficient arch to permit the water and its accompaniments to pass under free, and so constructed as yet to avoid causing an elevation to the present height of the main street.

There is a report afloat just now, that 18 laborers have absconded from the Island of St. Johns to the Island of Tortola, and that ten or twelve have lately been subjected to hard labour for an attempt at the same crime ? ? Such occurrences have happened in that Island repeatedly since the emancipation, and it is believed to a greater extent than before the emancipation. It is now asked, liow such occurrences can be reconciled with the proclamation of freedom and tho existing laws, and liow they can be reconciled with the interests of this Island, where such things could not happen :

Liins of flic Arctic! We have received American Papers to the 19th October. They give a detailed account of a most fearful collision that took place on the 27th September at noon, in lat. 46 o þÿ45 N., and Ion. 52 © W., when the American steamer Arctic was lost, and three hundred persons met with a watery grave!! This is most appalling ! ! ! The vessel which came in collision with the Arctic with such fatal consequences was the French propeller T esta, of 240 tons and sixty horse power. The weather was very foggy at the time, when the sad disaster happened, and the captain of the Arctic believing the ship to be uninjured, he endeavored to rescue the lives of those on board the Vesta, which vessel he thought was sinking. He had to return quickly to his own vessel, when alas ! lie witnessed the sad destruction which has thrown the city of New York in deep distress. The Vesta reached St. Johns, New Foundland, on the 30th September, very much injured, and with a loss of thirteen men.

As regards the provision laid down in the draft, that the salary of the Judge (Landfoged) on the event of vacancy, shall be reduced to $ 1 ,000 besides an official residence, the Colonial Council presume, that so considerably reduced a salary would not ensure the requisite capability for the office, the duties of which although less extensive than the other jurisdictions in these islands still requires to be executed with the same conscientiousness as all other places. | With respect to the official residence we think, as regards the interest of the State-treasury, that it would be more expedient, that the .1 udge, as hitherto, continues to partake in the expenses in keeping it in repair, by which means a guarantee will be had that this is done properly and economically ; according to the resolution of the Ministry of Finances, dated 11th Juno 1853, the Judge will henceforth until the year 1804 have to pay the State-treasury $156 annually in part payment ol the amounts advanced in the years 1849 to 1852 for work done to the official residence. Futhermore we deem it proper, that a certain amount be fixed (as done at the other jurisdictions) as a remuneration for office and travelling expenses or horses ; in this latter respect it must be observed, that out of the $800 fixed for policemen and conveyance, the present Judge receives $108 for travelling expenses, which makes his total annual income at present $2,348. As persons in the jurisdiction may be had for the appointment as po-

licemen, who on receipt of a proper remuneration Irom the Judge may assist in the writing, an amount ot $200 for office expenses and for keeping horses, which if it even do not quite cover the expenses of the office in this respect, may be somewhat sufficient. Regarding the amount $ 1 1 2,000 fixed for military expenditure, the Council can only refer to the remarks made in its report on the Budget for 1853-54 with respect to this item in general, and, with 1 0 votes against 6, agreed upon recommending that the contracts entered into for victualling the garrisons and for providing for hospitals be revised, and that there according to circumstances be advertised for written tenders, which is thought preferable to public licitation as proposed by the Committee. In regard of the sum of $10,000 for the establishment of a steam communication betweeu St Croix and St. Thomas, the Council is of opinion, that such an amount oilght not to be applied for the support of a private enterprise, which would never be satisfactory to the inhabitants or the public, and therefore, with 9 votes against 7, propose, that the $10,000 posted in Budget for

My Lord Duke: I have the honor to inform your grace, that the Allied troops attacked the position occupied hy the Russian Army, behind the Alma, on the 20th inst. ; and 1 have great satisfaction in adding that they succeeded, in less than three hours, in driving the enemy from every part of the ground which they had held in the morning, and in establishing themselves upon it. The Legislative Council met on Tuesday last for the despatch of public business, which terminated the following day, Wednesday the I till instant. # # The Militia Rill was brought forward and went through its first reading; at the introduction of this bill, his Excellency explained that the acceptance or non-acceptance of it by the Hoard would not influence Her þÿMajesty Government s either in retaining the Troops in the Island or withdrawing them from it ; after some opposition from the lion. Mr. Duboulay, the bill went through its first reading, subsequently it was read a second and third time ami passed. The qualifications were those of a Juryman, and the ages from 16 to 51). An Ordinance for establishivg a Court of Appeal to be held in the island of Barbados, was introduced by his Excellency for a first reading, with the intention of postponing the second reading

for a few weeks. His Excellency (according to theofficial minutes) was aware that the question had created some discussion, and was viewed unfavourably, and proceeded to show that instead of being so considered, it ought to be looked upon as a step of great advantage to the Colony, and one in every way calculated to operate beneficially. Hon. Mr. Macfarlane rose in opposition to the measure, stating his concurrence in the principle that an appeal from the decisions of a single Judge before a Court composed of three professional Judges to be preferable to the one in operation now in this Island, but unless that Appeal Court be a Circuit Court, it could never answer the end proposed; that the expense which would be incurred by suitors in appeal cases before a Central Tribunal at Barbados would be such, that the right of appeal would be practically denied except in cases where a large amount might be involved, that the difference in the laws respecting the rights of property be-

tween this Island and Barbados was another great objection to the scheme. The lion, member in concluding stated, that it was one of the most objectionable and unpopular measures ever brought before the Board, and that his Excellency must expect the determined opposition of the non-official section. As soon as Mr. Macfarlane resumed his seat, his Excellency stated in refer- j once to the opposition of the non-official members, that þÿ in that case, he should have to place two more Official Members at the þÿBoard, consequently with a view to force the measure by the weight of Executive pressure. þÿ Palladium, Oct. 14.

The Epidemic is still decreasing. Vieuxfert, l.aborie, River Doric, and Choiseul are free. The disease still continues at Soufriere, and in Castries every now and then some one is attacked. We understand that Cholera has broken out again at Canelle Estate with great violence. Heavy rains have fallen in town during the week to the benefit of the inhabitants as regards a supply of soft water, but to their injury on account of the damp and saturated state of the streets. þÿ Ibpt.

The Epidemic is flickering amongst us, reviving at one moment and dying away at the next. At Fond þÿd Or Estate, in the quarter of Deanery, there were a few fatal cases, the disease coming suddenly among the labourers after a very calm day and a few light showers of rain, and as suddenly departing. The last intelligence received from there (on yesterday evening) is exceedingly favourable, no new cases having occurred. þÿ Ibid, Oct. 21.

From the St. Iaicia Palladium Oclbr. 28. I. O C A b. The occurrences of the last week have stamped a new feature on our hitherto trodden down and passive people. The meeting which took place on Wednesday last according to appointment, was attended by some of the most respectable and influential of our inhabitants, and perhaps, at no period of this þÿIsland s history, has there been such firmness shown and good sense displayed in opposing a deservedly unpopular measure, as well as the absence of all rancorous feeling as exhibited itselfi 1 all the proceedings of Wednesday last. The time it appears has gone by when dissatisfaction only vented itself in useless grumblings, and when any measure, however unpopuliir and burdensome in its operation, would be received with that tacit feeling which sprung from a sense of utter helplessness; in other words, public spirit is resuscitated, and the people begin to understand their proper position, and will, doubtless, soon appreciate the doctrine that the most devoted loyalily and the highest possible public spirit are twin-sisters and ought to go hand in hand. The request about to be sent to the Lieutenant-Governor to stay all legislative proceedings on the Judicial Reform Question until Her þÿMajesty p s leasure be known on a Petition about to be forwarded, will, we suppose, convince our Rulers of the distastefulness of the measure, and unless a total disregard to the feelings and opinions of the Inhabitants be intended, little doubt can be entertained but what the concession will be made.
The rapid improvement of the health of the Colony has given parties interested in its affairs time to devote themselves to the accomplishment of measures which, if judiciously carried out,

| The Cholera continues its ravages in Port of Spain and San Fernando. In the former the number of deaths, as far as we can learn, averages more than 70 daily. In San Fernando on one day this week, 17 died, but since then about 8 per day has been the average. The Epidemic has not made much progress in the country districts in this portion of the Island. We are informed that 4 deaths have taken place at Garth Estate, and at two or three others there have been isolated cases : in the South Quarter there has been no case as yet. Preparations have been made at Savannah Grande, Victoria Village, and other places for affording medical assistance to the poor not resident on any Estate. The Colonial Council agree with the Government in regard of the dcsireabletiess of obtaining regulations in re, -poet to the position of the present Burgher Councils to the superior authoiities and their authority in regard of the administration of the economical affairs of the Municipalities, and also to obtain a change in the mode of election introduced during the lust year in St Croix and St. Thomas, according to which mode of election all the members of the Burgher Councils retire every year The drult bus been subjected to particular deliberation, and the Colonial Council beg leave to propose such amendments to the special paragraphs as have been agreed upon. ad I As the superior authorities in these islands must not only exercise coutrol over the economical administration of the communes, in like manner as that entrusted to the superior authorities in the mother country, they should also in certain respects take over the functions that are filled by the Magistrates in the mother country, and in other respects must have a greater authority than the superior authorities in Denmark, as many cases, that may there be laid before the Ministries, here cannot bear such delay ; the Colonial Council have unanimously with 17 votes considered it proper to recommend, that the conclusion of this paragraph þÿ under the inspection of the Commandant, as far as concerns the two

last mentioned islands, and otherwise with regard to all the islands, under the inspection of the Government and the Ministry of þÿFinances lie altered thus: þÿ under the inspection and superior administration of the superior authority ; add to which Council unanimously propose as an amendment to the commencement of the paragraph, that the words: þÿ together with the small islands thereto þÿbelonging be altered to : þÿ and the islands thereto þÿappertaining, þÿ and that the words : þÿ elected for each separate þÿisland lie altered thus: þÿ elected for the þÿsame. ml $ 3 After a strict deliberation of the conditions for the elective franchise, which according to the existing relations ought to be demanded, the Colonial Council beg leave, unanimously with 17 votes, to recommend, that this paragraph lie altered thus : þÿ The elective franchise is due to every mau rtf unblemished character, who has attained the age

8 Ji <© a 5S. A T a s of 3o years, and is in uncontrolled possession of his Estate, and : a, either has the communal rights accorded by a burgherbrief, and can prove that lie has an annual income of $500, or contributes at least $5 in ground and building tax to the State Treasury of a property in the commune belonging to himself or of a lease by recorded contract for a term of at 'east 5 years, or in St. Thomas, that lie pays at least $12 Trade or Store Tax to the Land Treasury ; b, or without regard to his being in possession of a burghersbrief or not, that he contributes at least $S annually in Ground and Building Tax to the State Treasury of property as above mentioned.

Any property that, according to what is stated above, gives a right to the franchise and is owned bv several persons in partnership, the elective franchise is only due to one of them, to whom the other part-owners transfer their right to this intent, provided such partner possess the qualifications þÿrequired. ad 4. We beg 1 cave, unanimously with 16 votes, to propose, that this paragraph be altered thus : þÿ Eligible as member is every man in possession of the franchise, who contributes at least $S annually in ground-and-building-tnx to the State Treasury of property in the commune, subject to the regulations relative to lease for several years or to partnership contained in paragraph 3, þÿ or in St. Thomas pays at least $ 10 annually in Trade or Store Tax to the Land Treasury. The person in question must also be domiciled in the | commune and have been residing there at least 1 year before lie can he þÿelected. ad 5 We propose unanimously that to this paragraph be add' d : i þÿ If two men, who stand towards each other in any of the above relations be elected at the same time, only that one of the two who receives 1 the most votes shall obtain the seat, and in case of any equal number of votes, drawing of lots shall decide which of the two shall obtain the seat ; the other one must be considered as not þÿelected. ail 6. The Colonial Council consider it proper, that the provisions in the draft relative to the election of substitutes should be omitted, especially because, on a vacancy occurring, it is desirable and

in accordance with the wish of the inhabitants to who can take the scat as representing a certain portion of the special interests of the commune, or possessing a certain kind of knowledge, and therefore unanimously with 16 votes recommend, that the paragraph be altered thus: þÿ The members of the Burgher Council are elected by those entitled to vote by plurality of votes and the number elected is to officiate 4 years in St. Croix and three years in the other islands. After the publication of this ordinance a general election of all the members of the Burgher Council shall take place. At the expiration of each succeeding year two members for St. Croix and two for St. Thomas and one tor St. Johns resign, and a new election of an equal number of members is to take place ; in regard to which of the members simultaneously elected are to resign, this must lie decided by mutual agreement, or in default of this by drawing lots ; otherwise it must he observed as a rule, that those members whose election is of the remotest date retire first. The members retiring may be re-elected. If a vacancy occur during the course of the year, a new member is to lie elected. Sueli new election, occasioned by a vacancy ocurring during the last 3 months of the year may however he postponed until the regular election that is to take place at the expirat ion of the year, provided that circumstances according to the opinion of the su-

perior authority or the Burgher Council do not demand, that the vacant seat lie filled previously The person elected instead of a retiring member ;s only to serve for the remaining period for which such retiring member was elected. The regular yearly elections ought to take place in such due time, that the result can be published within the expiration of the year, and the term of service to be reckoned from the first of January In the particular case mentioned below in paragraph 14 where an entirely new Burgher Council is to be elected, the members retire in like manner as stated above, relative to the members elected at the first general election, according to the provisions in this ordinance. ad 7 With reference to the analogy of the provisions of the Colonial Law, and as it must lie considered proper, that the jurisdiction of Frederiksted elect a certain number of the communal representative body, the Colonial Council, with 12 votes against 5, propose, that the words: þÿ Each island constitutes a separate election þÿdistrict he altered to: þÿ The island of St. Croix shall constitute 2 elective districts according to the jurisdictions ; that of Christiaustcd electing 5 and that of Frederiksted 3 members, and each of them one deputy member for the Burgher Council. The islands of St. Thomas and St. John constitute each an elective þÿdistrict, and that the words in the 6th line : þÿ elective þÿdistrict be altered to : þÿ Commune. A minority of 0 members must however de-

cidedly disrecommend that there be elected representatives separately for the jurisdictions of Christiansted and F rederiksted. The island of St. Croix compose, and according to the existing relations and especially the perfect identity of the interests of the country districts can only constitute one commune ; while the public institutions and the disbursements, that concern the Burgher Council, particularly also the poor establishment, arc common as regards the whole island, private affairs, þÿ such as those relating to merchants, administrators of estates, lawyers and medical practitioners þÿ are liy no means confined to the civil jurisdiction þÿ (as regards the policedepartment, the centre district, of the island, comprizes a separate jurisdiction) þÿ in which the parties concerned have not got their residence ; that the election takes place in both towns, is solely based in consideration of the convenience of the electors ; Imt the view of the elections is, to obtain the most capable individuals to take obtain a person in lieu of the retiring member, I charge of the interests of the commune ; þÿ nor has any tendency been shown at cither of the places to vote principally for persons residing in the same jurisdiction. þÿ A division like that proproposed by the majority would tend to establish a divergence of interests, and still, if this even be presumed, would in no manner aid the smaller jurisdiction which is to be represented in the Burgher Council with 3 against fi.

If oven the intention he, that the qualification of being elected at each place should not he dependent of the residence of the person elected, there would by a scattering of votes be caused considerable inconveniences, particularly thereby that persons residing in the country, the election of whom may he generally considered desireable, would perhaps not receive a sufficient number of votes at either of the elections, þÿ or also, if such a person be elected at both places, a re-election would bo requisite. All that can he done in this matter, although probably superfluous, would be, that among the members of the Burgher Council at least 1! ought to lie residents in the jurisdiction of Frederiksted , a subsidiary amendment to this intent was however not put to the vote in the Colonial Council ad 8. A late St. Thomas Paper, received here this morning brings the intelligcnce, which is copied from a California (San Francisco) Paper, of a battle between the combined Fleet and the Russians off the harbour of Pctropoloski on the 20th of August. The Russians lost about one hundred men and the F rench and English about sixty including three French officers. The fleet captured three Russian merchant vessels, one the ship Sitka, of 700 tons, and a schooner loaded with stores, which was destroyed after her cargo and crew were taken þÿ 100 men were taken prisoners from these vessels. The fact was learned from these men that the whole of the Russian licet, with the exception of the Dwinaand Aurora were in the sea of Ochotsk, at the mouth of the A moor, which river was in the Chinese possession, hut has recently been taken possession of by the Russians who have erected a palace and made a naval rendezvous at its mouth.

We recently took occasion to show that, while the Government of England was meritoriously anxious for the suppression of Slave ry and the Stave Trade, it was guilty of some strange inconsistencies in carrying out its object. The people of England were called upon to pay a large sum of money lor the emancipation of the Slaves in our own Colo nies ; considerable sums of money were oc cnsionally paid to Spain and Poitugal to in duce those countries to forego the carrying trade in Slaves, and to enter into treaties with England for its suppression þÿ treaties which, it is unnecessary to tell our readers, were no sooner paid for and entered into than they were violated. A considerable annual expense was incurred in maintaining a naval force on the coast of Africa to intercept the vessels engaged in the Slave Trade; yet. while all this was doing, a powerful stimulus was given to t he extension of Slavery by our legislation, which, for the first time, opened the best market in Europe þÿ IheBr ilish inai kei þÿ to t fie sugar produced by Slave labour in foreign countries. This conduct, we say, was strangely inconsistent on the pail of the Government of such a country as England, the sincerity of whose people in wishing to see Ihe Slave Trade abolished throughout the world could not be doubted. Such conduct was calculated to excite a suspicion on the part of foreigners that our Government was not really sincere in the desire it expressed

Mr. A. believes he shall discontinue his paper, because it contains no political news ; while B. is decidedly of opinion, that the same paper dabbles too freely in the political movements of the day. C. þÿdon t ake it, because it is all on one side ; and D. whose opinion it generally expresses, does not like it, because it is not severe enough upon the opposition. E thinks it does not pay due attention to fashionable literature. F. cannot bear the flimsy notions of idle writers. G. will not suffer a paper to lie upon his table which ventures to express an opinion against slavery. H. never patronises one that lack moral courage to expose the evils of the day. I. declares he does not want a paper filled with the hodge-podge doings of the Legislature. J. considers that paper the best which gives the greatest quantity of such proceedings. K. patronises the papers for the light and lively leading which they contain. L. wonders that the press does not publish þÿDewey s sermons, and such other solid matter. M. will not even read a paper that will not expose the evils of sectarianism. N. is decidedly of opinion that the pulpit, and not the press, should meddle with religious dogmas. O. likes to read police reports. P. whose appetite is less morbid, would not have a paper in which these silly reports are printed, in his house. Q likes anecdotes 11. wont lake a paper that publishes them, and says that murders and dreadful accidents ought not to be put into the papers. S. complains that his miserable paper gave

no account of that highway robbery last week. T. says the type is too small. U. thinks it too large V. stops his paper, because it contains nothing but advertisements. W. wants it to see what is for sale. Report to BSis Majesty. The Government has fixed before the Colonial Council the draft of the Budget for the Danish Westindia Possessions for the Financial year 1854-55, in consequence whereof the Council beg leave to state the following remarks : The Colonial Council consider it a want in regard of the form, that it only now at so advanced a period of the year for which this Budget was meant to lay down the leading rules, has obtained an opportunity of expressing its opinion, and that almost the whole year will have expired before it can be sanctioned, so that the Budget . for the previous year is extended far beyond the original period for which it was intended to be valid, and therefore recommend, that the Budget ! should in future be laid before the Colonial Council in so good time, that it, after having obtained royal sanction, could be put in force from the commencement of that period during which it is
extraordinary circumstances have caused the draft for 1854-55 being produced so late. As regards the Revenue-Side the Council are of opinion, that we ought to refer to its declara-

year 1853-54, purporting, that several of the existing taxes require to be remodeled, but that this is not practicable without at the same time remodeling the entire system of taxation. From the expressions of the Governor at the meeting of the Colonial Council we have gathered, that rather extensive preparatory labors have already been gone through for the re-organisation of the taxes, and we are therefrom justified in entertaining the hope, that we within a short time will be furnished with proposals relative to the re-organisation of the taxes. Under these circumstances we abstain from any further criticism of the Revenue-side, but would yet especially point out the inconvenience of the Vendue-Fee flowing into the royal treasury, which as a tax on. the daily transfers of property from man to man, is apt to check and impede commercial undertakings, when it becomes necessary to realize stocks of merchandize on hand ; we must likewise animadvert against the fees of the lower courts, which in many cases are extremely irksome, and arc not collected according to the same rules in the different jurisdictions. In passing over the Expense Side Council shall confine itself strictly to those items, which appear to merit particular notice. Ad Chap : II. B 1 . In regard to tho amounts $192 aud $128 fixed for the Inspector of public buildings at Christiansted and Frederiksted, we must refer to what the Colonial Council in its report on tLe Budget for 1853-54 has remarked regarding the desirableness in future of uniting

these offices to that of Inspector of Roads whenever it becomes vacant, just as it is at present united to the office of Surveyor, while perhaps other duties, such as : the Inspection of the Harbor, Wharves and Landing Bridges in Christiansted and Frederiksted could also bo attached hereunto, and thus a sufficient income be obtained I produce a bad for a scientific Civil Engineer, the want of which is so very much felt in these Islands. In regard to Chap II B 2. Concerning the regulations of the Judiciary and Police Department, in St. Croix in general, we can find nothing to object to, as we suppose that the functionaries mentioned in the draft will be able to attend to

far as it is projected, eventually to transfer to the Judges þÿ who are also to act as police-masters þÿ the functions of the Judge Advocate, we are in- ! duoed to observe, that just as much as this func-

þÿtionary s time on the one hand in some cases will be taken up to the injury of his other important duties, in so much will he on the other hand be exposed to au unsuitable position of dependence on the Military. The Council must dissuade such a combination, and therefore, with 14 votes against 4, propose, that tho duties of tho Judge Advocate in St'. Croix, until a proper alteration be introduced relative to the treatment of the military court cases, on a vacancy occurring, be made over to one of the lawyers in each term on a suitable remuneration. With regard to the expenses connected with the contemplated regulation of the Judiciary and Police Department, Council is of opinion, that the salary for the Police-master at Kingshill fixed at $1800 besides $300 for travelling expenses is too small, which the Government also seems to acknowledge, having observed in the moiives, that as far as the State Treasury is concerned no larger amount can be granted. Council also thinks, that when as a necessary regulation we must continue a distinct Police J urisdiction for the extensive Centre District, the necessary aid of an Assistant ought to be granted to the functionary, who is to conduct the same. Council therefore, with 15 votes to be law ; we must however acknowledge, that i against 3, propose that the salary and travelling expenses to the Police-master at Kingshill be fixed at respectively $2000 and $300, in all $2300, and with 12 votes against 6, that there be granted $960 for an Assistant at the same

tion in the report on the Budget for the financial | Jurisdiction, on condition that in such case $160 be deducted out of the $600 þÿallow ed for stationary. The increased expences for the Police-jurisdiction of the Centre District will in this manner be in all $1000, of which amount $700 may bo made up by deducting something out of tho sum fixed for the Sheriff' and Police-master in Frederiksted, being the same as that fixed for the like functionary in Christiansted, viz. : salary and travelling expenses $2900 and office expenses $3000, because the business is of less extent in the Jurisdiction of Frederiksted. The Council therefore, with 12 votes against C, beg leave to propose, that the salary and amount of travelling expenses be fixed respectively at $2400 and $300 and for office expenses $2500. As regards the sum fixed in the draft for Policemen and þÿ þÿGensdarmcs, wo would observe, that already in the report on the Budget for 1853-54 tho Colonial Council had cause to disrecommend an arrangement whereby soldiers yet on tho roll aud receiving pay and rations from the respective garrisons bo made use of as Policemen. In referring to what has been advanced on this subject, Council bog leave to add, that it is not presumed necessary to apply Policemen armed aud organised on a military footing in countries where order and quiet reign. Even if Government may have thought that the introduction of the new laws affecting the relations of tho country population may have oc-

casioned any disturbances of order making tho police force necessary, we nevertheless do not think that there does now exist any reason to entertain such thought. In like manner as it, according to the opinion of competent military men, will have an injurious influence in tho military discipline, that soldiers bo commanded to perform civil police-service ; so likewise will no adequate advantage be obtained from tho þÿGensd armes, who by their presence impression on peaceable people, and easily þÿ particularly on account of their unacquaiutanco with the language of tho people þÿ might on given occasion bo tempted to use their arms without necessity. Should the police require an incrcaso of its force, and it bo desired to have persons from tho garrison, it would probably be preferable, that, , as hitherto adopted, such persons obtain leave of the duties attached to their offices Only in so i absence from the military service and be consi- dered civilians ; while on the other band tho military should only render assistance to tho police under military command in the same manner as has heretofore been customary. Sometime after flour got scarce and the baker learning that the Merchant to whom his had been sold had some on hand, went out and after taking out the plugs of one barrel and tasting the flour, putchused the whole at twelve dollars and a half per þÿbarrel and brought it away with him. On opening the first barrel however and taking oil the top of the flour, he found to his consternation that he had bought back his own bad flour and given one dollar and a Itaif per barrel more than it was sold for þÿ sosurptised was he and fancying it to be a judgement, he fell upon his knees and vowed never again to practise a cheat þÿ a vow we hope he will religiously keep. þÿ St. Vincent Gazette.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL Second Session Report to Hi Majesty. (Continued.) Ad Chap. II. C. I. A minority consisting of 5 members from St. Thomas consider ourselves justified iu observing, that we do not deem it absolutely necessary, that St. Thomas is provided with a superior authority termed President or Vice Governor, who together with the secretary's and bookkeeper's office attached to it, require an annual outlay of 12,340 dollars. In this respect we take the liberty to state, that the Colonial Council in its last session, with a majority of 13 votes against 5, proposed, that the said superior authority should be discontinued, which the Government at that time thought practicable, under certain conditions, especially a steam-communication between St. Croix and St. Thomas. From what has since transpired in the matter we have not found sufficient reason to consider such a reform inexpedient. According to our opinion, equipoise between the revenues and disbursements would be obtained in a more convenient manner, than by clipping some few hundred dollars from the salaries of subordinate officials, by which means one will arrive at this result, that in time to come efficient men cannot bo had from the mother country to fill the offices, the more so because tho salaries are now not greater than what is deemed suitable to tho office In as far as it is stated in the Government's preambles, that the late occurrences, during which tho communication between St. Croix and St. Thomas has been very much limited, and tho administra-

tion of St. Thomas and St. Johns has been almost exclusively intrusted to tho Commandant, has proved tho necessity of retaining such a superior functionary, we beg leave to observe, that what is here stated by Government is scarcely of so much consequence as therefrom could be inferred. Even whilst tho Cholera Epidemic prevailed, to which we suppose allusion is made, tho transmission of letters could notwithstanding just as well as heretofore be carried on ; and as regards the internal arrangements in the island of St. Thomas with respect to tho opidemio, tbero has not, as far as wc know, been dono anything more than what tho Commandant and the Board of Health, in which tho Burgher Council had a scat and vote, had by exebango of letters agreed upon, and which could have been performed in a shortor time without any Commandant-office, by the Town Judge in his capacity of magistrate presiding in the Commission. How little importance can bo attributed to tho administration of the Commandant appears more clearly from certain facts, such as, that ho could not allow that a person arriving from England during tho prevalence of tho Cholera Epidemic immediately could procood to St. Croix, or that a box of medicines could bo forwarded there without spocial permission previously obtained from tho Government in St. Croix. In as far as the preambles go to show, that the President in his capacity of Vice Governor shall take charge of tho Government at St. Croix in caso of the death of the Governor or his depar-
ture, such an arrangement appears desirablo if such

a functionary is to bo retained in St. Thomas ; j but "von without this arrangement there scarcely j wi1! arise any difficulty in said respect, as the Governor in ease of his departure can make arraneementa beforehand in regard to his successor, and in the event of so extraordinary a case as h;s doah, which has not yet taken place s ice the reoccupation in the year 1815, the Commander of the forces who next to the Governor holds the highest military command may very well for a few months, until another Governor can take i charge of the Government, with the assistance of the Government's Secretary attend to the administration, as during this interval there can be no question of any new enactments of pervading importance. Should however the Government consider it requisite that a superior authority be in the island of St. Thomas, in such case the minority deems it more expedient to have the seat of the Government with its Secretary's and Bookkeeper's offices at St. Thomas. We do not tliiuk it requisite that these 3 small islands have more than one superior authority, and we are of opiuion that the nature of the relations demand, that the Governor ought to have his residence in St. Thomas in preference to St. Croix. The sphere of action in the lastmentioned island is almost exclusively confined to Agriculture, and consequently what appertains to the same is there of paramount importance. In as far as the Government can and ought to legislate for these, it may be said that nearly

everything is regulated by law, in the emanatiou ' of which the Representatives of the islar. have taken an active part. To watch over the execution of these laws we presume may easily be done from St. Thomas, especially if the Governor should at times inspect St. Croix, which must be premised as a natural consequence ; nor do we suppose there will arise questions which demand an immediate settlement by the Governor, since the country population in general is disposed to quiet and order, and on the whole live under better relations than the laboring population in other countries, where labor and its ultimate results aro of characteristic importance. In St. Thomas on the contrary all interest is attached to Commerce and Shipping, on which the relations with Europe as well as with this part of the world exercise an essential influence. Royal Society of Northern Antiquaries. The annual meeting of the Society was held at the castle of Chrisiinr.xhorg, Copenhagen, on the 7th May. His Majesty the King of Denmark presiding. The Secretary and Councillor of State, Professor Charles C, Rafn, submitted a report of the Society's proceedings fot the past year (1853) and laid before the meeting a new volume of the " Annals of Northern Antiquities and History," which contains þÿ 1st. The Saga of King Edward the Holy, with Danish translation, compiled by C. C. Hafn and Jon Sigurdson j 2d, Geographical elucidation of Scotch and Irish names of places as they occur in the Sagas, by P. A. Munch, of Christiana ; 3d. Save of Upsala; 8 to 9, On the alloy of northern metal and its connexion with that of ancient bronzes, ql c., by N. J Berlin, of Lund; 10 to 11, On the Danish Runic stone of the 11th century, found in ti e middle of London, and observations upon Gorin the ancient and Thyra

sir, ©iRass Danabod's monument in Jellinge, by C. C. Rafn ; 12th, Appendix to the historical account of Soeborg which appeared in a former volume, by C. F. Wegener. This volume is embellished with 14 plates and other illustrations. At His Majesty's request Councillor Rafn communicated his interpretation of the inscription on the monumental stone of Gorm the old, King of Denmark, in Jellinge, and observed that he had been so fortunate, with the assistance of the parish clergyman, Superintendent Kemp, whose frequent examination of the stone, under various lights, had enabled him to discover several marks not previously observed, as to be able to fill up the most important of the blanks in the concluding line, which was not entirely legible to the previous interpreters 1'iofessor Rafn gave the following interpretation; þÿ "King llat aid caused this mound to he raised to (the memory of) his father, Gorm, and his mother, Thyre, that Harald who conquered the whole of Denmark and Norway, and christened the Danish people." Several steel engravings of weapons of bronze for the previously announced ' Atlas of Northern Archaeology," were exhibited, and 12 sheets had been printed of the Old Northern Poetical Dictionary, of Sveinbiorn Egilson. His Majesty communicated the recent discovery of remarkable objects in the village of Skiaviogcin Seeland, on the excavation of a drain to conduct the water from a tutfmoor. On the edge of this, lying upon yellow sand, having turf underneath, five pieces of cut flint,

iu the form of hnlfirtoons, were found. The discovery was rendered rematkable from the manner iu which the flints were placed, being in the form of a caltrop, four of them making a cross, while the fifth stuck upwards from the centre. This unusual disposition of the flints appealed to His Majesty to be wot thy of observation.

The King then communicated some antiquarian and historical elucidations with respect to the old Abrahamslhorp, which Councillor Wegener had executed at his Majesty's instigation, and now read to the meeting, and the King recommended that they should be published in the Society's Annals of Northern A rehaeology and History. Mr. Browne, of London, had transmitted a drawing and description of a grave stone, with Runic inscription, found in St Peter's Church-yard, Dover. He considered it lobe a monument of the Danes, and evidence of their appearance in Kent, which led htm to make the communication to the Society. Professor Rafn exhibited two photographs of the marble lions of Venezia from the Pit us us, upon which Runic inscriptions are cut. At his instance, Ferdinand Bertouch Esquire, long resident at Venezia had undertaken a minute examination of those inscriptions, and has already collected valuable matter for future discussion

From the St. Thomas Times, October 1 1 . Steamers for the West Indies.

From the New York Courier and Enquirer." A Bonus of $15,000 a year, for seven years, having been voted and guaranteed by the Legislature of the Colony of British Guiana, for the purpose of aiding in the establishment of direct and regular steam communication between the port of Demerara and the United States, and official assurances of corresponding sums having been received from various paKs of the West Indies, it is proposed by certain American, English and West Indian gentlemen (should sufficient encouragement be offered), to commence the contemplated line with a first class steam-ship of at least 1000 tons burthen. It is arranged that the ship shall be monthly in her communications, touchins, going and coming, at Bermuda, St. Thomas, Barbados and Denierara ; and affording every possible facility that time and distance will allow, to the adjacent Islands and ports of the South American Continent. It is arranged also, that the line shall regularly connect at St. Thomas with the steamers now arriving there from VeraCruz, Chagres, Jamaica the Windward Islands, and Southampton; while its arrivals in and departure from the United States shall he made to correspond with those of the different European lines. The important facilities afforded by this new medium of communication must at once bo obvious to the commercial world. Opportunities for the certain transfer of freight, for the speedy transmission of letters, and for the convenient passage of travellers, will thus be se-

cured, which, it is confidently believed, must eventually command the patronage of the public, with a bonus of $30,000 a year, to back it. In view of those facts, it is respectfully requested that those to whom this Circular is sent shall signify their wishes with regard to the proposed line. It is presumed that all underwriters will find it to he for their interest to contribute to its support. CommunicationsshouUi be addressed to Charles W. Dennison, II. S. Consul for British Guiana, at Philada.

A POPULAR MOVEMENT IN DENMARK (From the Illustrated London News, Sep 9 ) Public opinion in Denmark is beginning to manifest itself against the Government in a soraei what ominous manner. Those who have been watching the struggle going on there between the Danish Court party and the people will remember that, in July last, the Cabinet issued a Constitution octroyee, providing chiefly for the establishment of a Consultative Chamber of Notables About the same time the Constitutional party, whose leaders in Parliament bad suffered proscription at tho hands of Government, formed a Constitution Society, to promote its views by argument, and to enforce them by public opinion The peculiarity of the ease was that the vast ma jority of the Parliament voted a want of confidence in the Ministry, and tho Ministry replie d

a by dismissing the Parliamentary leaders, and decreeing a new Constitution. The Danish Parliament was to open on Saturday last. Four days before its opening, an immense meeting of the Constitution Society was held in the elegant theatre called the Casino þÿ the largest hall in Copenhagen. Government had forbidden all political meetings in the open air, but it could not hinder 3000 patriots from assembling on Tuesday week, to protest against its tyrannical conduct. The meeting comprised the elite of the moneyed world, of the journals, the bar, the universities, and the people. There was not much speaking, but what was said was to the point. The whole proceedings were characterised by unquestionable unanimity and great moderation of language. They condemned the ordinance of the 26th July as a violation of faith with the people, and as unconstitutional ; they hinted at the dangers which might result from the Ministerial policy ; and they pledged themselves to support the parliament in defending the rights of the nation. The resolutions were couched in general terms ; but that their purport should not be mistaken, Mr. Broberg, the largest shipowner in Denmark, distinctly put it to the meeting whether they perfectly understood that the resolution implied the impeachment of the Ministry and the refusal of taxes He was answered by a storm of applause and a unanimity of affirmatives, which appeared endless ; hats and handkerchiefs adding their confirmation. THE U. S. AND THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC. Translated from La Cronica. We have received direct advices, from what is called the Spanish part of St. Domingo, down to 26th of last month. Everything appeared tranquil ; and the very fact that our friends make no mention of any hostile act or threat on the part of the black empire against the Dominican Republic, seems to indicate that Soulouque had suspended his aggressive plans, whether for reasons of his own or for those suggested by the political and mercantile interests of England and France, to which no questions of peace in America can be indifferent, while they are involved in war in Asia and Europe. Our correspondent therefore tells us nothing of threats or invasions. On the a contrary, everything, they say, wears thy particular pacific aspect, though not or of mention the less wor- of the attractive observation of those who have political or other interests to attend to in the Archipelago of the Antilles. Letters from the city of St. Domingo tell us of the arrival at that port of the U. S. frigate Columbia, on the 17th of July, with Gen. Cazenau on board, and a Commissioner of this Government, with powers to make a treaty with the Dominican Republic. As tar as could be collected from the first proceedings, the treaty was to have for one of its various ostensible objects, to stipulate for certain rights in the ports of the Republic, and especially in the spacious and secure bay of Saniana, for the armed vessels of the United States, in case ot war, and in time of peace for the estab-

lishment of a kind of colonization, black or white, of individuals from the United States in some part of the Dominican Republic. The frigate Columbia had been in a manner established at Samana, under pretext of waiting were Chambers, which until the Dominican in session, should approve the convention ; and it even appears that the intention had been expressed of remaining until the ratification by those of the government of the United States. In the meantime the speedy arrival of the American ship-ofwar Albany was spoken ot, and also a war steamer; and by way of pastime, an officer of engineers on board the Columbia was assiduously engaged in making charts of the bay and peninsula of Samana. Nothing, apparently, can cause less alarm than the presence of an American negotiator, with one, two or three vessels-of-war of the same nation, in any part of the West Indies; but, most antecedents of the apparently as the innocent act may afford us ground for forelow, telling the consequences concealed and the somewhat which may fol- spirit which may have produced it, and as the occurrence we have mentioned not only has some remarkable antecedents, but may well be a symptom of the re-appearance, in the political sphere, of the course constantly pursued hy the democratic administrations of the U. States, at epochs of disturbance and conflicts in Europe, it would be proper perhaps not to neglect, as a frivolous or unimportant thing, a demonstration which, especially in present circumstances, may perhaps

s tr> © m <s» a ss. a t a s» We have with great care, been collecting in our paper for several years the facts which reveal a certain tendency of the politics of this Government to make St. Domingo the point of support for some future enterprise, for the injury of the present European dominion in the West Indies; and, as a first step, to carry into effect the precept of Monroe, which is here regarded almost as an oracle for truth. The idea, as we have been able to infer it, and as we have often expressed it, is this: the European dominion being established in the West Indies, and supported by formidable means of defence and offence for a case of war, and there existing, also, in many of those Islands, a strong national spirit, the employing of force against those groups of population would be entirely ineffectual; and, if it were so, it would never give a result which would repay the sacrifices it must cost It is necessary, therefore, for the United States to avoid all apparent responsibility in the first aggressions by which a serious civil conflict may be produced in any of those groups, or between any of them. The United States then, by applying their peculiar nations lic law and the law of doctrine of pub- with respect neutrality to and harbor and protection in the ports of the Union for the contending parties, indiscriminately whether thecontest arose between sovereignty and sovereignty by right , or between a subject or province in rebellion against its sovereign, the United States without com-

promising themselves nationally in the contest, might favor the party for which they felt most sympathy, in all the moral and material means of war. Canada and all Spanish America at different periods have given eloquent testimony of the perseverance with which the United States have observed to the letter that strange doctrine proclaimed without disguise, by their Presidents and statesmen, and established in their law books. None of the foreign interests affected by it have ever protested formally against it until now, as, although Fox and Ashburton skilfully defended, in favor of England, a case of its application, they did not attack it in principle, nor establish in a clear and conclusive manner the determination that the precepts established by the general public law of Europe should be observed in America. Spain, who, of all nations in contact with this country, is the one who ought to have most strongly protested against the innovation introduced hy the American government in the case of intercourse and the international duties, has likewise done nothing that we know ot, on her part, although we have full confidence that this question will be satisfactorily elucidated by her present it wor- an thy representative in Washington, occasion should present itself. The Federal Administration then, consider themselves masters of the perfect right to interfere neutrally (if we may use such a phrase) in contests of the kind referred to, without compromising I

the peace of their country, and deriving, from any foreign state of hostility, either promoted by them or not, all the advantages of national war, without any of its losses or disasters. Heretofore they . ish America, directly from their own have raised in revolt Canada and Spanterritory, against their respective sovereigns; but this method is falling into disuse, and presents some dangers, since the pretext has been declared inadmissible of the alleged insufficiency of the Federal laws to restrain those who arm and go forth, &c., from the territory of the U. States, against the territory of any foreign nation, prince or colony. It was necessary, therefore, to abandon

the old system, and seek other territory from which the same ends mny be reached, without the dangers which would arise from such direct sallies as those of the Creole and the Pampero. It would be useless for lis to insist on our well-founded conviction that the island of St. Domingo is not the point chosen by the policy of neutral intervention. Its physical structure and geographical situation, the quality of its harbors, and, above all, the weakness of the two nations which occupy it, and the continual hostility prevailing between them, are circumstances which favor the realization of the plan of this nature, and presents to American policy a cup full of brilliant, but, in our view, illusory hopes. The presence of the American ship of war in the bay of Samana, its significant operations, the project of a treaty, and the renewal of the old and persevering plan of colonization, (of which we have said so much in our paper,) þÿ all of these objects which have inspired a degree of alarm in our zealous and faithful correspondents, may well have sonic relation to some design worthy of particular investigation, if not of a formal and direct declaration from the maritime powers, especially those liable to be effected by a serious change in the present political equilibrium of the Antilles. The population of SI. Domingo, white and colored, are also deeply interested in this question, because the pivot of the question is their extirpation or their life. Judging from precedents of this kind

in America we can have little to hope from the intervention of England in the case. France has the mission and the duty of requiring an explanation of the movements which may tend to endanger her possessions, and to restrain the freedom of her navigation in future. Few statesmen, perhaps, have come to the New World who were as penetrating and good statisticians as her present representative in the United States.

It is highly amusing to see with what pertinacity a writer in the " Avis" of the 3d instant comes forth to lecture not only the Planters anil Managers on the aU-ahsorbing topic of changes among the labouring classes, during the months of July and August, but like- , wise the ministers of religion in this Island. This "Comical Genius," after referring to materials for a farce, vacation months for the Policemasters, Weeding Machines, and Plough Con- 1 tracts, four, five and ten dollars a head, very deliberately delivers over the Planters and Managers to a reprobate sense, as incorrigible beings with whom in future he will have nothing more to do as it would he labor lost, and in order to gain notoriety he turns round and gravely charges the Clergy, merely on hearsay, or rather "we have heard things whispered about," with injustice, with tampering and intermeddling with the people and prevailing on them to withdraw their notices to quit. This self-sent dogmatizer his undertaken a very serious mission, he reminds one of a certain Sandy Mc'Swish who has lately made his appearance in America. In default of credentials for ordination Mr. Sandy has assumed the high sounding cognomen Angel Gabriel to impose on poor credulous dupes (and it is supposed he has some sane people amongst his followers) by pretending that he was sent byGod to teach and preach and to remind people of the great sin of injustice &c. Mc'Swish or as he is now called, the Angel, was born in the Isle

of Skye, after being miraculously saved from being drowned in a little pool called the Devil's Loch, lie turned his attention to the stage and joined a company of equestrians, which occupation he followed for some years. Having quarrelled with the manager this budding angel turned his thoughts to a a more se- rious business and became self-commissioned preacher, he entered on his new vocation with so much earnestness that he sometimes alarmed his simple hearers, whom he used to arouse from their apathy by blowing a tremendous tin horn from the pulpit. After practising in England for sometime Mc'Swish found himself at length in New York with just money enough in his pocket to purchase a brass trumpet and with this for his stock in trade, he has commenced the Angel Gabriel line of business which has proved so highly profitable and made his name so famous. With all due submission we would recommend "Comical Genius" to adopt die Angel's system to procure an instrument singular in construction and composition to Lis and continue blowing into the ears of the Planters nnd Managers ruin I destruction! desolation! until they desist fromtheir abominable practico þÿ lie may even succeed in bringing back those that have left him if any. As for the clergy tie may rest satisfied that they will not interlere without some reasonable cause, such as the advising laborers, who are ignorant of the practice, fiom going to a place wheie it is known the slick will be brought

to bear on their beads, if they attempt to come forward with complaints concerning wages &c &c, It may be that tiie ministers of religion have exerted their influence in controuling in a measure, the corrupt system of bribery so much complained of They may be even solicited by old parents, who are tottering on the verge of the grave to assist them in prevailing on their unnatural children not to quit them because they know by the experience of the last six years what treatment they may expect in their new domicile when once they leave the old ones If "Comical Genius" considers this interference on the part of the clergy unjust or unfair we beg leave to differ from him and if he should obstinately persist in his opinion lie

Mr. Editor ! A desire to benefit the rising generation tempts me to address a few words to them or their parents, through the columns of your paper. Of late we see numberless youths, of all classes, who, so soon as they leave schitol, immediately strive to enter either a store, office or some other so-called gentlemanly occupation, instead of going forth in the world, where they may make choice of an occupation, which will place them, when j I old age arrives, in an independaut position. Trades are despised by them ; and they are encouraged by their parents to look on the position of a gentleman-clerk (poor fellow !) as the acme of existence They fail to see, and their parents are likewise blind enough not to perceive, that " Honour and shame from no condition rise." It is true, our tradesmen, with some exceptions, are not an enviable class of the community. Bad habits, unfair competition, and an old-schoolsticking to high prices take the bread out of their mouths daily ; and make their lives anything but enviable. I certainly never could council that parents should recommend such a life to their children ; but this I say, that if they learnt trades, nnder j the eye of their parents, and then proceeded to such rising and prosperous countries as Australia they would fiud a bright career open to them. It will not answer for parents to ask, where the means are to come from to give their | children to reach such distant places. Where there is a will there is a way ; and it parents

would but turn their attention to emigrants from | other countries they would see that the bulk oi thera is from among the poorer class I never can see a youth enter a storo or office, without sighing to think that one more unfortunate has been encouraged by bis parents aDd friends to enter on a career as aimless as the existcnec <5f a savage. No doubt bright visions of $10 or the like, float before their youthful eyes, ! and make the many years of apprenticeship pass lightly, until this goal shall is have But when this golden dream once realized, and been attained manhood attained, together with a strengthening of those bonds of association and love of home, which might have been sundered at an early age without any pain to the individual, hut which have now attained a cable's strength, he then finds that he has fully entered on a career of life without prospects and subject to all the bitterness of subordinate situations, without the slightest hope of amelioration. To a young man of any capacity, however small, such a life is of all to be most dreaded : he arrives at manhood, and finds that the period which might have been spent in an other country in acquiring a respectable position in society, with a prospect before him as wide as his mental eyes may choose to paint, and realizable too, if he only possesses energy enough to struggle for its attainment, for it is a truth, which we learn from the lives of all truly great men, that whatever a man wishes to bo, he can become, þÿ he finds I say, that this pe-

riod has passed, ties have become strengthened and still he continues in his low, unaspiring because he dares not aspire) position, where all his endeavours arc now directed, not to better that position, but only to deserve his hard earned pittance. Whom must he thank for this ? I am sorry to say that I cannot find any other persons on whom the blame can bo attached but his parents. They were his natural councillors, and they, if they do not, which is very likely, continue in their blindness, must thank themselves for having caused the brightest energies of their offspring to lie dormant and suffocated in tho narrow sphere of his existence.
