(Continued ) Whenever it should become necessary for the Government to take steps for the protection of this interest, it is plainly seen, that if the Governor resides at St. Thomas, which forms a point of concentration for the Steam communication between Europe as well as between places in the Mexican gulf, he will by speedy decisions do more good than if ho resided in St. Croix, which would occasion loss of time, often to the injury of the case. In liko manner the Governor on the occurrence of any case can act with greater promptitude by residing at St. Thomas, siuco he by being on the spot can render himself conversant with the various relations in a more perfect manner than if he should bo obliged to receive such knowledge through the medium of declarations and the like from others. Neither ought this circumstance he overlooked, that tho Governor by residing at St. Thomas in consequence of the relations established by steam postal communication is drawn nearer the rest of the civilized world, which iu regard to him in most cases will amount to a half and in other cases to a whole month. If any weight is to bo attached to matters of representation, then it is indisputable, that the Governor ought to reside at St. Thomas where strangers arrive, and not at St. Croix where nouc come. The Majority of the Colonial Council, consisting of 12 members, among which both the members for St. Johns, can by no means concur with tho minority's ideas respecting the unnecessari-

ncss of the office of tho superior-authority at St. Thomas and St. Johns, and must therefore refer to the reasons stated by the minority of 5 members in the Council's most submissive report on the draft of tho Budget for 1853-54 against tho proposed dissolution of the said office of tho superior authority, the correctness of which reasons has been confirmed by experience of the last years. The superior authority of said islands was, during tho period of the devastating Cholera Epidemic, tho authority that effected and conducted all those contrivances that on the part of

the public had to he attended to immediately on the sud 1 u outbreak of the calamity, and by tho application of extraordinary energy and indefatigable tie ss obviated great increase of the horrors, and with particular vigilance not oniy attended to the benefit of those islands, but also in a high degree maintained the Government's endeavors to prevent the contagion being carried over to St. Croix, and all this could only ho effected by an authority, that according to its position has been presiding over all the rest on the spot, and thereby been enabled to maintain that unanimity without which tho sphere of action of the different officials an l other authorities, under such extraordinary relations, would otherwise terminate into confusion and disagreement. Should Government during the period in question have given orders, according to which no travellers or articles could, without its sanctiou, be conveyed from the said infected islands to St. Croix, which restrictions how vcr during the discussions in the Colonial Council has been contradicted as not quite correct, can have no influence on arguing the point with regard to the position of the superior authority beyond its own sphere of action ; þÿ and with respect to what lias been alleged by the minority, that the transmission of letters can always be carried on, the Colonial Council must observe, that the communication by letter at that period was considerably limited in consideration of tho security of tit. Croix, and

moreover it is not through tho means of communication by letter, but by the personal appearance and activity, that the superior authority under such circumstances has to conduct the relations. A later occurrence has also confirmed what has been alleged in the nbovcraentioncd report of tho Colonial Council as a reason for the continuance of tho superior authority at St. Thomas, viz : tho relations with regard to the Commanders of the foreign men-of-war frequently arriving there, settlement of the affair of the British vessel " Fan- as it must be considered a fact, that the fortunate ny's" being fired into from onoof the batteries in St. Thomas in the presence of the English Stcarnfrigatc "Calypso," which might otherwise have given rise to very considerable inconveniences and loss to the State, is solely attributable to tho conduet and promptitude of the superior authority, and that no subordinate authority could either bavo obtained such an arrangement, or even bad the competency to put it into execution, notwithstanding every thing depended on an instantaneous decision. With regard to the opinion hitherto entertained, that the establishment of steam communication between these islands might possibly be of some moment in respect to deciding tho question relative to the discontinuance of the office of tho superior authority at St. Thomas, the Colonial Council must observe, that what is stated above no doubt sufficiently goes to provo, that no alleviation whatever of the communication between

the islands can render the personal presence of the superior authority superfluous, and moreover tho distance is so great, that an express in extraordinary eases, even by the means of a steam vessel, would he too late, without regard being had to such periods when tho repairs of the vessel or of tho machinery may offer obstacles. The Colonial Council cannot but consider it inconsistent in the minority, after having declared the office of the superior authority in St. Thomas superfluous, to propose subsidiarily tho removal of tho scat of Government from St: Croix to St. Thomas. As f.i as we know, this is a new idea, which would scarcely he welcomed excepting at St. Thomas, wherefore we will not enter upon stating any other reasons against it, than that tho change would not tend to any retrenchment. The salaries of the Governor and the other officials on their removal to St. Thomas would have to be considerably increased on account of the greater dearncss of tbc place. Now buildings would have to be erected tor the Governor and tho secretary's oflico J-c. Moreover, according to what has been stated during the discussions, a civil director of affairs would have to he appointed in St. Croix, and as this official must have his officers besides a royal treasury's office ij-c., tliis change would actually terminate in the Government being removed to St. Thomas, and tbc office of the superior authority to St. Croix attended with greater expense, in consequence of the greater number of the officials who

Electricity v. Cholera. þÿ Mr. Meinig, of Leadenhall street and 213 a Piccadilly, who some time ago introduced a very ingenious small apparatus, called the" Electro Generator." by which, when worn on the body, mild currents of electricity are communicated to the system, has found that this simple means constitutes a very effectual preventive and check to the premonitory symptoms of cholera. Mr. Meinig asserts that, during the Inst visitation in the north, not one single person who wore an " Electro Ge- " nerator was attacked by cholera ; and that, within the last few days, he has himself witnessed the greatest possible benefit derived from its application in cases of diarrhocu, &c As there is no inconvenience whatever attendant upon the wearing of this small portable apparatus, and the little known of the nature of cholera points distinctly ton certain connection between it and the electric stato of the body and atmosphere, it is not improbable that in electricity may be found the means of counteracting this dreadful scourge, and the oUser vations of Mr. Meinig are well worthy the attention of the profession and the public at large.
